keyboard.intro: An input is one tab stop and takes the keys of a native text field: typing, selecting and system shortcuts are the browser's.

rows.action: Moves focus into and out of the field. A disabled field is skipped; a read-only field keeps its place in the order.
Sends the form that holds the field. If a required field is empty or wrong, focus goes to the first one and its message shows in a tooltip.
In a field with `type="search"` the browser clears what was typed. In other types it does nothing.
With `revealable`, Tab moves from the field to the show-or-hide button; Space or Enter shows or hides the password. Focus stays on the button.

behavior.intro: What the input does itself, and what it leaves to the page.

items.title: A native element
items.text: Input renders a native input, so every attribute works (type, name, value, autocomplete, pattern, required and the rest), and refs reach the element.

items.title: Controlled or not
items.text: Pass a value and change handler to own the text, or a default value to let the field keep it. Inside a Field, the description and error are linked to the input for assistive technology.

items.title: Size and density
items.text: Size sets the height: 32, 36 or 40 px at the default density, 36, 44 or 52 px in comfortable density. They match the Button heights, so a field and a button line up.

items.title: Label
items.text: A label joins the text to the field, and when the field is disabled the label and helper dim with it. A field without a visible label takes an aria-label and renders the bare input.

items.title: One component, two shapes
items.text: With no field props, Input renders just the bare input; with any, a column of label, field and message. Props count by being present, so toggling an error never swaps the DOM or drops focus.

items.title: Invalid
items.text: An error turns the border and focus ring red and shows its message in place of the helper. The fill stays white, and both messages are linked to the input.

items.title: Password reveal
items.text: A revealable password field gets a show or hide button in the trailing slot, with a label and icon that follow its state. It does nothing on other types.

items.title: Validation tooltip
items.text: On submit, the first field that breaks a rule gets focus and the browser's message shows in a WunderUI tooltip, not the browser's bubble. It clears as soon as the person types or leaves the field.

items.title: Disabled and read-only
items.text: Disabled dims the field to 40 %, skips it in the tab order and leaves it out of the form data. Read-only stays readable, focusable, copyable and submitted, with a subtle fill.

items.title: Content inside the field
items.text: Leading and trailing put an icon or text inside the field, drawn in an InputGroup that holds the border and focus ring. For a button or shortcut you compose yourself, use InputGroup by hand.

items.title: Loading
items.text: There is no loading prop. Put a Spinner in the trailing slot, set aria-busy and keep the field editable, so a background check never blocks typing.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The border colour changes quickly when the pointer enters or the field takes focus. Nothing moves or scales.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the colour change stays as a short fade, since it isn't movement. The spinner in a loading field stops turning.

minimalUsage.expected: You see the label Work email above a white field with a grey placeholder. Clicking the label focuses the field and turns its border indigo.

parts.name: Progress
parts.description: The root: a progressbar with its min, max and current value set, and children such as the label render above the bar. The value can sit right or left of the bar, below it, or in a bubble.

parts.name: ProgressLabel
parts.description: Names the task, and Progress points to it as its label. Without a label, give Progress an aria-label.

parts.name: ProgressIndicator
parts.description: The fill, in the brand colour, drawn at full width and scaled to the value so it glides to a new one. Progress already renders it; with a null value it has no width.

parts.name: ProgressTrack
parts.description: The grey bar behind the fill: 6 px high and fully rounded. Progress already renders it; you only need it for a custom layout.

parts.name: ProgressValue
parts.description: Prints the formatted value, a percent of the range by default, in tabular figures. It is hidden from assistive technology, because the bar already announces its value.

parts.name: ProgressRow
parts.description: One line of a breakdown, such as a rating distribution or the share of a channel: the label with an optional icon, an 8 px bar and the share at the end. The row reads as one image. It replaces HistogramBar.

items.text: Use Progress for a task that runs to completion: an upload, an import, a run of setup steps. For a fixed value inside a range, such as storage used, use Meter.
Name the bar with a label, such as Uploading report.pdf. Screen readers then say what is progressing, not only the number.
Add the value part when the number matters. It formats the value in tabular figures, so the text does not jump while it counts.
Put the value where it is read first: right for a compact row, bottom when the bar spans the full width, or a bubble when the number should follow the end of the fill.
Set the max to the number of steps when the task has steps, and pass the steps done as the value, such as 3 of 5. The bar then needs no sum of its own.
When you print your own text, also pass a value text for screen readers, such as 3 of 5 steps. Otherwise it announces the percent.
Say a failure in words next to the bar and offer the next action, such as Failed, retry. The bar keeps the value where the task stopped.
Don't animate the width of the fill yourself. The indicator already scales smoothly.
Don't use an indeterminate bar for a long wait on its own. It draws no fill and no motion, so pair it with a Spinner or a message.
Don't show a bar for a measured value such as storage used, since it would announce a task that is never finished. Use Meter.

useFor: A task that runs to completion and whose progress you know, such as an upload or an import
A run of steps, such as a setup checklist, with the count of steps done as the value
A queue where every item has its own bar and its own status

useInstead.name: Meter
useInstead.text: a measured value inside a range, such as storage used or a quota

useInstead.name: Spinner
useInstead.text: a wait of unknown length that has no value to show

useInstead.name: Skeleton
useInstead.text: content that is still loading into a layout

behavior.intro: What the bar does itself, and what it leaves to the page.

items.title: Role and value
items.text: Progress is a progressbar with a min (default 0), a max (default 100) and the value clamped to that range. The announced text is a percent of the range by default; you can replace it.

items.title: Accessible name
items.text: The bar has no name of its own: a label inside it becomes the name, and without one you pass an aria-label. The value part is hidden from assistive technology, so it is never the name.

items.title: Indeterminate
items.text: A null value marks a bar whose progress is unknown. The fill has no width and nothing moves, so show activity another way, with a Spinner or a message.

items.title: Complete
items.text: When the value reaches the max, the parts are marked complete; below it, progressing. The bar does not change colour: say that the task is done in the label.

items.title: Size and tone
items.text: One size and one tone: the track is 6 px high and fully rounded, and the fill uses the brand colour. There is no error variant, so tell a failure in words next to the bar.

items.title: Value position
items.text: With a value position the value sits in a 40 px column right or left of the track, below it, or in a dark bubble that follows the fill. The bubble is hidden from assistive technology.

items.title: Motion
items.text: When the value changes the fill glides over 700 ms and only the transform moves; the first render draws it at its value without moving. The bubble moves to its new place at once.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the fill jumps to its new value. Colour changes stay.

minimalUsage.expected: You should see the label Uploading report.pdf above a bar that is half full, with 50% at its right.

Progress.value.description: How far the task has come, between `min` and `max`. A value outside the range is clamped. `null` marks the bar indeterminate: it has no `aria-valuenow` and draws no fill.

Progress.min.description: The value at which the bar is empty. The default is 0.

Progress.max.description: The value at which the task is complete. The default is 100. Set it to the number of steps to count steps.

Progress.valuePosition.description: Prints the value with the bar: `right` or `left` in a row with the track, `bottom` below it, `tooltip-top` or `tooltip-bottom` in a bubble that follows the end of the fill. Leave it out to place `ProgressValue` yourself among the children.

Progress.format.description: `Intl.NumberFormat` options for the value. Without them the value is printed as a percent of the range; with them the clamped value itself is printed, as in `{ style: "unit", unit: "megabyte" }`.

Progress.locale.description: The locale for the formatted value, such as `de-DE`. The default is the locale of the browser.

Progress.aria-valuetext.description: Replaces the text a screen reader announces for the value. The default is the formatted value, or `indeterminate progress` without a value.

Progress.getAriaValueText.description: Builds the announced text from the formatted value and the raw value, such as `3 of 5 steps`. It is called with `null` as the value while the bar is indeterminate.

parts.name: Slider
parts.description: Holds the value and draws one thumb per value: a number gives one thumb, an array of two gives a range. It offers several thumb styles, a centred fill, a value bubble, tick marks and an error state.

parts.name: SliderLabel
parts.description: A visible name for the slider, linked to the thumbs, placed with the value in a row inside the Slider. SliderField draws its own label.

parts.name: SliderValue
parts.description: Shows the current value or range on the right in tabular figures.

parts.name: SliderControl
parts.description: The area that takes pointer input, a little taller than the track so it is easy to hit. Slider already renders it.

parts.name: SliderTrack
parts.description: The grey bar the thumbs travel on, 6 px thick, horizontal or vertical. Slider already renders it.

parts.name: SliderIndicator
parts.description: The filled part of the track up to the value, or between the two thumbs of a range. A centred slider fills from its origin.

parts.name: SliderThumb
parts.description: The handle people drag or move with arrow keys, Home, End, Page Up and Page Down, and the element screen readers announce. It takes the page tone on hover and the subtle tone while dragging.

parts.name: SliderBubble
parts.description: The decorative value bubble above the thumb. It fades in on focus and while dragging, and thumbs close together share one.

parts.name: SliderMarks
parts.description: Decorative tick marks on the scale. Label only the marks that need a word, never every step.

parts.name: SliderField
parts.description: A slider as a form field: a label that names the thumbs, the current value with its unit, optional limits, number inputs and helper or error text. An error turns the slider red.

parts.name: SliderInput
parts.description: A number field that follows the slider, uses the English number format, and clamps and snaps when you leave it.

parts.name: SliderRangeInputs
parts.description: Two number fields for a range. The lower value may not pass the upper one.

items.text: Use it when the rough position matters more than the exact figure: volume, a price range, a zoom level. For an exact number use a Number Field.
Use SliderField for every slider in a form or panel, so the label and current value always sit next to the thumb. Add number inputs when exact values matter.
Name every slider: SliderField takes a label and a bare Slider takes an aria-label. A range is announced as Budget, minimum and Budget, maximum.
Set the step to the precision people need and keep the large step at about ten steps. Shift with an arrow key, Page Up and Page Down move by the large step.
Pass an array such as 20 and 80 as the value for a range. The slider draws one thumb per value.
Label only the marks that need a word, such as the first, the default and the last. A label on every tick is noise.
Show an error through the error prop: the fill and thumb turn red and the text is announced. Say what to change, like Choose at least 10%.
When a slider is disabled, give the reason in the helper text. The value stays readable, and people shouldn't have to guess why they can't change it.
Don't add SliderThumb children for a range. The array decides how many thumbs there are.
Don't rely on colour alone for an error. The red fill comes with the error text and an invalid state for screen readers.
Don't use a vertical slider without a height. It fills its container's height, so a column without one gives the track nothing to stretch to.
Don't use a Slider for a choice between a few named options. Use a Segmented Control or a Radio Group.

useFor: Choosing a value where the rough position matters more than the exact number, such as volume, opacity or zoom
Choosing a range between two values, such as a price or an amount
A value on a scale around a middle point, such as a balance from -100 to +100

useInstead.name: Number Field
useInstead.text: an exact figure that people type or step with buttons

useInstead.name: Radio Group
useInstead.text: a choice between a few named options, such as Day, Week and Month

useInstead.name: Progress
useInstead.text: showing how far a task has come, where people cannot change the value

keyboard.intro: Every thumb is a native range input, so the browser handles focus and arrow keys, and the slider adds larger steps. A range has two tab stops, the lower thumb first.

rows.action: Moves focus to the next or previous thumb. A disabled slider is skipped.
Raises the value by one `step`.
Lowers the value by one `step`.
Moves the value by `largeStep`, ten steps by default.
Raises or lowers the value by `largeStep`.
Jumps to the minimum or to the maximum. In a range the thumb stops at the other thumb.

behavior.intro: What the slider does with its value, thumbs, states and motion.

items.title: Controlled or not
items.text: Pass a value and a change handler to control it, or a default value to let it keep its own. A commit handler runs once on release or key press, which is the place to save.

items.title: One thumb or two
items.text: A number gives one thumb that fills from the minimum, and an array of two gives a range where the lower thumb never passes the upper one. A click on the track moves the nearest thumb.

items.title: Centred
items.text: Centred draws the fill from the middle of the scale, or from a number you pass, and marks the zero point with a short line. It works for one thumb only, and a range keeps its normal fill.

items.title: Vertical
items.text: A vertical slider fills the height of its container, with the maximum at the top and the bubble beside the thumb. SliderField draws no error text for it, though the slider is still marked invalid.

items.title: Bubble
items.text: The bubble fades in while the thumb has focus or is dragged, or always if set. Range thumbs closer than 15 % of the scale share one bubble, and screen readers get the value from the value text.

items.title: Marks and limits
items.text: Marks are decorative ticks under the track, and only the step snaps the thumb. Limits show the lowest and highest value under the ends.

items.title: Value text
items.text: A format function sets the text of the value, bubble and screen reader value, so $25 is announced as $25 and not as 25. Without it values use the English number format, such as 1,200.5.

items.title: Disabled
items.text: A disabled slider is drawn at 40 % opacity, is not focusable and ignores the pointer. The value stays readable.

items.title: Invalid
items.text: Invalid or an error turns the fill and thumb red and marks the thumbs invalid. The error text is an alert and describes the thumbs.

items.title: Hover and dragging
items.text: The thumb fills with the page tone on hover and the subtle tone while dragged, and the cursor becomes a grab hand. The thumb follows the pointer directly, without trailing.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The thumb changes its fill with a quick colour transition, and the bubble moves 4 px and fades in and out. Only opacity and transform animate.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the bubble does not move, it fades in place. Nothing else moves, because the thumb follows the pointer.

minimalUsage.expected: You see the label Volume on the left and 40% on the right, above a track filled up to 40 % and a round thumb you can drag or move with arrow keys.

Slider.value.description: The value of a controlled slider: a number for one thumb, an array of numbers for a range. Pair it with `onValueChange`.

Slider.defaultValue.description: The starting value of an uncontrolled slider: a number for one thumb, an array of two numbers for a range such as `[25, 75]`.

Slider.onValueChange.description: Called on every change while the thumb moves, with the new value (a number for one thumb, an array for a range) and the event details.

Slider.onValueCommitted.description: Called once when a change ends: the pointer is released or a key is pressed. Use it to save instead of saving on every move.

Slider.min.description: The lowest value on the scale. The default is 0.

Slider.max.description: The highest value on the scale. The default is 100.

Slider.step.description: How far a value moves with one arrow key press, and the grid the thumb snaps to while dragging. The default is 1.

Slider.largeStep.description: How far a value moves with Page Up, Page Down or Shift with an arrow key. The default is 10.

Slider.minStepsBetweenValues.description: For a range, the fewest steps that must stay between two thumbs, so they can never touch. The default is 0.

Slider.orientation.description: `horizontal` runs across the container and is the default. `vertical` runs up a column that has a height, with the maximum at the top.

Slider.disabled.description: Dims the slider to 40 % and takes it out of the tab order and out of pointer input. The value stays readable.

Slider.handle.description: The shape of the thumb: `circle` is the brand-outlined default, `circle-neutral` has a grey rim like a plain button, `grip-bars` and `grip-dots` are a rounded drag item.

Slider.centered.description: Fills from the middle of the scale instead of the start and marks the zero point. `true` uses the middle of `min` and `max`, a number sets the origin, such as `centered={0}` on -50 to 50. A single value only.

Slider.bubble.description: Shows the value in a bubble above the thumb (beside it when vertical) while it has focus or is dragged. `"always"` keeps it on screen. Close range thumbs share one bubble.

Slider.formatValue.description: Turns a value into the text shown in the bubble, beside the label and in `aria-valuetext`, such as `(n) => "$" + n`. The default is the English number format.

Slider.marks.description: Tick marks under the track. A number is a tick, `{ value, label }` also names it. Label only the ticks that need a word. The marks are decorative.

Slider.invalid.description: Marks the slider invalid: the fill and the thumb turn red and the thumbs get `aria-invalid`.

Slider.error.description: Error text under the slider. It is announced, linked to every thumb through `aria-describedby` and marks the slider invalid. For a vertical slider the text is not drawn; use `SliderField`.

Slider.thumbClassName.description: Extra classes for every thumb, for example to change its fill.

Slider.thumbAlignment.description: How the thumb sits at the ends of the track: `center` puts its middle on the end of the track, `edge` keeps the whole thumb inside it. The default is `center`.

Slider.thumbCollisionBehavior.description: What two thumbs do when they meet: `push` moves the other thumb along, `swap` lets them trade places, `none` stops the dragged thumb at the other. The default is `push`.

Slider.format.description: `Intl.NumberFormat` options for the number shown in the bubble and in `aria-valuetext`, such as `{ style: "currency", currency: "USD" }`. `formatValue` wins when both are set.

Slider.locale.description: The locale for number formatting. The default is `en-US`, so 1200.5 reads as 1,200.5.

Slider.name.description: The name the value is submitted under when the slider is inside a form.

Slider.form.description: The id of the form the slider belongs to, when it is not inside that form in the markup.

Slider.className.description: Extra classes for the element. A function receives the state and returns the classes.

Slider.style.description: Inline styles for the element. A function receives the state and returns the styles.

Slider.render.description: Replaces the element with another element or component, or composes it with one. It takes an element or a function that returns one.

SliderField.label.description: The visible name of the field. It names every thumb (`aria-labelledby`). Without a label, use `Slider` with an `aria-label`.

SliderField.value.description: The value of a controlled slider: a number for one thumb, an array of numbers for a range. Pair it with `onValueChange`.

SliderField.thumbAlignment.description: How the thumb sits at the ends of the track: `center` puts its middle on the end of the track, `edge` keeps the whole thumb inside it. The default is `center`.

SliderThumb.index.description: The position of the thumb in a range: 0 for the lower one, 1 for the upper one. `Slider` sets it for you.

SliderThumb.handle.description: The shape of this thumb. See `handle` on `Slider`.

SliderThumb.invalid.description: Puts `aria-invalid` on the range input inside the thumb.

SliderThumb.aria-valuetext.description: Text that says what the value means, such as `$25`, when the number alone is not enough for a screen reader.

SliderThumb.getAriaLabel.description: Returns the accessible name of the thumb from its index, such as `(index) => (index === 0 ? "Minimum" : "Maximum")`.

SliderThumb.getAriaValueText.description: Returns the `aria-valuetext` of the thumb from the formatted value, the raw value and the index.

SliderThumb.inputRef.description: A ref to the hidden range input inside the thumb, the focusable element.

SliderThumb.tabIndex.description: The position of the thumb in the tab order. The default is 0.

SliderThumb.onFocus.description: Called when the range input inside the thumb gets focus.

SliderThumb.onBlur.description: Called when the range input inside the thumb loses focus.

SliderThumb.onKeyDown.description: Called when a key is pressed on the thumb, before the slider handles it.

SliderThumb.className.description: Extra classes for the thumb, for example a different fill.

SliderInput.min.description: The lowest accepted value. A smaller value is set to it when the field is left. The default is 0.

SliderInput.disabled.description: Dims the field and takes it out of reach.

components.title: Pagination
components.description: Page navigation with Prev/Next and numbered pages, or a simple "Page X of Y" mode.
components.props: function Pagination({ page, pageCount, onPageChange, className, shape, showEdges, currentStyle }: PaginationProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: currentStyle
props.description: Figma "Current style": the current page in the brand colour or on a subtle surface. Default "primary".

props.name: shape
props.description: "pill" rounds every button fully (Figma Shape=Pill). Default "rounded".

props.name: showEdges
props.description: Adds "First page" and "Last page" as their own buttons at the two ends.

props.name: onPageChange
props.description: Called with a valid page (a whole number from 1 to `pageCount`).

props.name: buttonLabel
props.description: Text of the button. Default "Go".

props.name: label
props.description: Visible label. Default "Go to page".

props.name: value
props.description: Current page size.

props.name: label
props.description: Visible label. Default "Rows per page".

props.name: options
props.description: Choices in the menu. Default 10, 25, 50, 100.

props.name: shape
props.description: "pill" rounds both buttons fully. Default "rounded".

props.name: errorMessage
props.description: Shown instead of the default message while `status="error"`.

props.name: itemCount
props.description: Rows on the current page, for an unknown total or a short last page. Defaults to `pageSize`.

props.name: noun
props.description: Singular noun for the total, "result" in "248 results".

props.name: nounPlural
props.description: Plural noun, defaults to `noun` + "s".

props.name: onRetry
props.description: Makes the error state show a "Retry" button.

props.name: page
props.description: Current page, 1-based. Together with `pageSize` it gives the range "1–10".

props.name: pageSize
props.description: Rows per page.

props.name: status
props.description: "loading" shows a skeleton, "error" says the count failed and offers a retry.

props.name: total
props.description: Total number of rows. Leave it out when the total is not known.

parts.name: Pagination
parts.description: A nav named Pagination with Prev and Next around numbered page buttons. You hold the page and change it in the page change handler; options are shape, current style and first and last buttons.

parts.name: Edge buttons
parts.description: The first-page and last-page buttons at the two ends, shown with the edges option. Each is an icon button named First page or Last page.

parts.name: Prev and Next
parts.description: Text buttons with a chevron: Prev is disabled on the first page and Next on the last. Below 640 px the text hides and the chevron stays, and screen readers still read the text.

parts.name: Page button
parts.description: A numbered button that goes to its page. The row always shows the first page, the last page and the pages around the current one.

parts.name: Current page
parts.description: The page you are on, marked as the current page. Primary fills it with the brand colour, subtle sets it on a quiet surface.

parts.name: Ellipsis
parts.description: Stands for the pages that are folded away. It is plain text, not a button.

parts.name: PaginationSimple
parts.description: The compact form: Previous and Next with a Page X of Y label between them, for narrow spaces. It takes the same shape.

parts.name: PaginationSummary
parts.description: The count line: a range of a total (21 to 30 of 248), the total alone, a range without a total, a loading skeleton, or an error with a Retry button.

parts.name: PaginationPageSize
parts.description: A labelled select for the number of rows per page. Its label is the accessible name of the select.

parts.name: PaginationJump
parts.description: A labelled number field with a Go button. Enter or Go jumps to the page; a value outside 1 to the page count shows an error under the row.

items.text: Keep the page in state and load the matching rows in the page change handler. Pages count from 1, and the page count is the total number of pages.
Show where people are with PaginationSummary next to the pager, such as 21 to 30 of 248. When the total is unknown, leave it out and it says Showing 21 to 30.
Reset the page to 1 when the page size, a filter or a search changes. Otherwise people can land on a page that no longer exists.
Use PaginationSimple where only Previous and Next fit, such as a narrow card or a phone, and keep the count in PaginationSummary above the list.
Don't build page buttons by hand. Pagination already disables Prev on the first page and Next on the last, and marks the current page.
Don't show a pager for one page. With a page count of 1 it shows a lone 1; hide it instead.
Don't use Pagination for a feed that grows as people read. A list that appends more rows needs a Load more button or an infinite list, not pages.
Don't let the page leave the range 1 to the page count. Pagination does not clamp it, so a stale page shows a row with no current number.

useFor: Long tables and lists where people need to reach a specific page, such as invoices or members
Search results, where position matters and people go back to a result they saw
Server-side data, where every page is its own request

useInstead.name: Tabs
useInstead.text: peer views of one object, not pages of one list

useInstead.name: Breadcrumb
useInstead.text: the path of a page inside the product

useInstead.name: Carousel
useInstead.text: a few slides or cards that people move through one at a time

keyboard.intro: Every control is a native button, field or select, so the browser provides focus and activation.

rows.action: Moves focus to the next or previous enabled button. A disabled Prev or Next and the ellipsis are skipped.
Goes to the focused page, or one page back or forward from Prev and Next, or to the first or last page from the edge buttons.
In the jump field: goes to the typed page. A number outside 1 to `pageCount`, or no whole number, shows an error and stays where it is. It does not submit a form around the pager.
In the open page size menu: moves between the sizes. Enter or Space on the closed select opens the menu, Enter chooses the highlighted size and Escape closes it.

behavior.intro: What the pager does with state, the page list, the edges and motion.

items.title: Controlled
items.text: Pagination keeps no state: the page comes from you, and every click reports the new number. Nothing changes until you set the page.

items.title: Which pages show
items.text: The first page, the last page and the current page with one neighbour each side always show, so the row holds at most seven items. Gaps fold into an ellipsis, which can stand for a single page.

items.title: Edges
items.text: Prev and Next are disabled on the first and last page: they keep their place, drop to 40% opacity and are skipped by Tab. The edge buttons follow the same rule.

items.title: Current page
items.text: The current page stays a button, so choosing it again reports the same number. Hover tints a page with the page background and pressed with the subtle one; the current page keeps its own fill.

items.title: Narrow screens
items.text: Below 640 px Prev and Next show only the arrow. The row never wraps and is about 340 px wide on a phone (412 px with edge buttons), so in a narrower space allow wrapping or use PaginationSimple.

items.title: Summary states
items.text: Loading shows a skeleton and announces Loading results. Error is an alert saying the count could not load, with a Retry button if you set a retry handler, and a total of 0 reads No results.

items.title: Jump errors
items.text: The error text of PaginationJump sits under the row without making it taller, so a form around it does not move. The input stays marked invalid until the next edit.

items.title: Numbers and direction
items.text: Counts use the English format with a comma, such as 1,248. The chevrons turn 180 degrees in right-to-left layouts.

items.title: Motion
items.text: Nothing slides: the current page changes in place. Page buttons change colour at the base speed; Prev, Next and the edge buttons a little faster.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: There is no movement to remove, so reduced motion changes nothing. The colour changes are short fades and stay.

minimalUsage.expected: You see a disabled Prev button, pages 1 and 2, an ellipsis, page 12 and Next, with page 1 filled. Click 2 or Next to move the current page.

PaginationPageSize.disabled.description: Disables the select, for example while a page loads.

PaginationPageSize.onValueChange.description: Called with the number of rows the person chose. Reset the page to 1 here.

Pagination.shape.description: `rounded` gives the buttons 8 px corners and is the default; `pill` rounds every button fully.

Pagination.currentStyle.description: How the current page is drawn: `primary` fills it with the brand colour and is the default, `subtle` marks it with a quiet surface.

components.title: Separator
components.description: A thin dividing line, horizontal or vertical, solid or dashed.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: orientation
props.description: The orientation of the separator.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

parts.name: Separator
parts.description: A 1 px line, horizontal by default and as wide as its container, or vertical and as tall as its row. It can be dashed, never shrinks in a flex row and has no margin.

items.text: Use it to divide groups inside one surface, such as two sections of a card. For a line with text like or use Divider with Label, and inside a toolbar use ToolbarSeparator.
Place a vertical Separator in a flex row that has a height. It stretches to the row, so without one the line has nothing to stretch to.
Use the dashed style for a lighter break inside one section, such as the line above a total, and the solid line between sections.
Leave the spacing to the layout: a vertical margin between sections, padding on list rows, and a gap in a row.
Make the line decorative when a heading, list or group already shows the boundary. Keep the default when the line is the only sign of it.
Don't draw dividers with a border class or a hex colour. Separator uses the border token, so it follows the theme and dark mode.
Don't use a Separator as a panel resizer, because it is not focusable and has no value. A resizable layout needs a splitter with keyboard support.
Don't stack a Separator on a border that is already there, such as the last row of a bordered list or a card edge. Two lines read as one thick one.

useFor: Dividing groups of content inside one surface, such as two sections of a card or the rows of a list
Setting inline items apart in a row, such as links, figures or toolbar groups
A lighter dashed break inside one section, such as the line above a total

useInstead.name: Divider with Label
useInstead.text: a line with a word, a button or an icon on it, such as or between two ways to sign in

useInstead.name: Toolbar
useInstead.text: a row of actions, which has its own ToolbarSeparator for splitting groups

useInstead.name: Card
useInstead.text: a group that deserves its own surface instead of a line around it

behavior.intro: What the separator does with length, style, semantics and motion.

items.title: Length
items.text: A horizontal separator is 1 px high and full width, a vertical one 1 px wide and as tall as its flex row, so put it in a row with a height. It never collapses.

items.title: Style
items.text: Solid fills the line with the border colour. Dashed draws a 1 px dashed border in the same colour, on the top for horizontal and the left for vertical.

items.title: Semantics
items.text: Base UI renders a div with the separator role and sets the orientation. Horizontal is the default and vertical is announced as such, and the line is not focusable.

items.title: Decorative
items.text: There is no decorative prop. Pass a presentation role and aria-hidden to remove the line from the accessibility tree, as Divider with Label does.

items.title: Spacing
items.text: The separator has no margin. Use a vertical margin between stacked blocks, padding on list rows and a gap in a row, so one rule sets the air for every line.

items.title: Theme
items.text: The colour is the border token in both styles, so the line follows the theme and dark mode with no extra class.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The separator has no state and no transition. Nothing in it moves.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: There is no animation to reduce, so reduced motion changes nothing.

minimalUsage.expected: You see a line of text, a 1 px line across the full 320 px width with 16 px of space above and below it, and a second line of text.

Separator.orientation.description: `horizontal` runs across the container and is the default. `vertical` runs down a flex row and stretches to its height. It also sets `aria-orientation`.

Separator.dashed.description: Draws the line as a 1 px dashed border instead of a filled line, for a lighter break inside one section.

Separator.render.description: Replaces the `<div>` with another element or component, for example `render={<hr />}`. The role and the orientation attribute are still set on it.

Separator.className.description: Extra classes for the line, such as a margin (`my-4`) or a fixed length for a vertical line (`data-vertical:h-5`). A function receives the state and returns the classes.

Separator.style.description: Inline styles for the line. A function receives the state, which holds the orientation, and returns the styles.

components.title: Divider with Label
components.description: A separator with a centered text label, e.g. for "or" between two sign-in options.

parts.name: DividerWithLabel
parts.description: A full-width row of a line, a label and a second line, separating two groups such as two ways to sign in. A small size suits a short word like or, and the lines can be dashed.

parts.name: Lines
parts.description: Two decorative lines that stretch to fill the space on either side of the label. With no label the row itself becomes a single separator and the two lines meet in the middle.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: A word or two such as or, centred between the lines in muted text. It can also hold a small plain button, an icon button or an icon.

items.text: Use a Divider with Label between two alternative ways to do the same thing, such as social sign-in and email. For a line without text, use Separator.
Keep the label to one or two words that say how the groups relate: or, or continue with. Longer text squeezes the lines away.
Place it only between two alternatives, such as sign-in buttons above and an email form below. The label reads as a choice between what is above and what is below.
Use the small size for a one word label such as or, and the default size for a phrase such as or continue with.
Put a small plain Button or an IconButton on the line for an action that belongs to the break, such as Load more. Give an icon button an aria-label.
Use the same word as the buttons around it. If the buttons say Continue with, the label says or, not alternatively.
Don't use it as a section heading. The label is small, muted text with no heading role, so start a new section with a real heading.
Don't put it above the first or below the last block. It separates two blocks, so with only one side it points at nothing.

useFor: Telling people that the groups above and below are alternatives, such as a provider button and an email form
A break in a long list that carries its action, such as a Load more button on the line
A short phrase that leads from one option to the next, such as or pay with card

useInstead.name: Separator
useInstead.text: a plain line, horizontal or vertical, without any text on it

useInstead.name: Heading
useInstead.text: the start of a new section, which needs a real heading element for screen readers

useInstead.name: Card
useInstead.text: two options that each deserve their own surface instead of a line between them

behavior.intro: What the divider does with its layout, its label and the lines.

items.title: Layout
items.text: The row is a full-width flex container with the items centred. The two lines share the space the label leaves, so the label always sits in the middle and cannot move to the start or end.

items.title: Size
items.text: The default size has a 14 px medium label and 12 px between label and line. The small size has a 12 px regular label and 16 px of air, which suits one word.

items.title: Label
items.text: Anything that is not empty counts as a label: text, a button, an icon. Null, false, true or only spaces count as no label, and then the gap is 0 and the two lines meet.

items.title: Semantics
items.text: With a label the row has no role and the lines are hidden, so a screen reader reads the label as plain text. Without a label the row is announced as a separator.

items.title: Interactive label
items.text: A button or icon button on the line keeps its own focus stop and name, in page order. The divider adds no keyboard behaviour of its own.

items.title: Theme
items.text: The lines use the border token and the text the tertiary text token, so the divider follows the theme and dark mode. A button on the line keeps the colours of its own variant.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The divider has no state and no transition. A button on the line has the hover and press motion of the button itself.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: There is no animation in the divider to reduce. The button on the line follows the reduced motion rules of Button.

minimalUsage.expected: You see one line across the full 384 px width, broken in the middle by the words or continue with in small muted text.

DividerWithLabel.children.description: The label between the two lines: a word or two, a small plain Button, an IconButton or an icon. Leave it out for a single separator.

DividerWithLabel.size.description: `default` has a 14 px medium label and 12 px of air on each side. `sm` has a 12 px regular label and 16 px of air, for a single word.

DividerWithLabel.dashed.description: Draws both lines as 1 px dashed borders instead of filled lines, for a lighter break.

DividerWithLabel.className.description: Extra classes for the row, such as a vertical margin. The row is a full-width flex container.

components.title: Skeleton
components.description: A pulsing placeholder shown while content is loading.
components.props: function Skeleton({ className, variant, ...props }: React.ComponentProps<"div"> & VariantProps<typeof skeletonVariants>): React.JSX.Element;

parts.name: Skeleton
parts.description: A grey placeholder with a soft sweeping highlight, as a 14 px text line, 20 px title line, 40 px avatar circle or 100 px block. It has no role or label and is still under reduced motion.

items.text: Use a Skeleton while content with a known layout loads: a list, a card, a profile. For a short wait on an action, such as saving, use a Spinner.
Give each Skeleton the size of the content it stands for. The layout then keeps its height and does not jump when the content arrives.
Make a text placeholder as tall as the line it stands for. The text shape is 14 px high and a normal line is 20 px, so add 3 px of margin above and below.
Draw what you already know, such as the table header or the card title, and put placeholders only where data is missing.
Mark the loading region as busy and remove that when the content is in. Add a visually hidden status line saying what is loading, because the placeholders say nothing to screen readers.
Show a skeleton for the first load only. When data refreshes, keep the old content on screen and update it in place.
Don't fill the whole screen with blocks. Cover what is visible when the page opens and let the rest render with its data.
Don't leave a skeleton on screen when loading fails. Replace it with an error message and a way to try again.
Don't build your own placeholder for charts. They have a loading state that draws a skeleton of the right height.

useFor: Content with a known layout that loads, such as a table, a list of members or the cards of a dashboard
The first load of a page or a panel, where an empty area would look broken
A region that fills with data and should keep its size when it does

useInstead.name: Spinner
useInstead.text: a short wait on an action, such as saving, or a panel without a known layout

useInstead.name: Progress
useInstead.text: a task that reports how far it has come, such as an upload

useInstead.name: Empty State
useInstead.text: a list that has loaded and has nothing in it

behavior.intro: What the placeholder does with shape, size, motion and assistive technology.

items.title: Shapes
items.text: Text is a full-width line with a 4 px radius, and title is a taller line two thirds wide. Avatar is a 40 px circle, and block, the default, is a 100 px box with an 8 px radius.

items.title: Size
items.text: The shape only sets a default. Add a width, height or size in a class to match the content, since your class is applied after the shape.

items.title: Line height
items.text: A normal text line is 20 px high and the text shape is 14 px. A 3 px margin above and below makes the placeholder as tall as the line, so the layout does not move when the text arrives.

items.title: Shimmer
items.text: The bar uses the muted colour. A highlight, 6 % foreground (10 % in dark mode), sweeps across from left to right every 1.8 seconds, without end.

items.title: Accessibility
items.text: The Skeleton is a plain div with no role or name, and it is not announced. Mark the loading region as busy and add a visually hidden status element that says what is loading.

items.title: Theme
items.text: The colours are tokens, so the bar and highlight follow the theme. The highlight is a little stronger in dark mode so it stays visible on the darker bar.

items.title: Motion
items.text: Only the highlight moves. The size, layout and bar colour never animate.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the highlight is not drawn. The grey bar stays, so the loading state is still visible, just still.

minimalUsage.expected: You see a grey circle with two grey bars beside it, a shorter one above a longer one, and a soft light band sweeping across all three from left to right about every two seconds.

Skeleton.variant.description: The shape of the placeholder: `text` for a line of body text, `title` for a heading, `avatar` for a round picture and `block` for an image or a chart. The default is `block`.

parts.name: Tooltip
parts.description: Holds the open state and links the trigger to the label. You can control it, switch it off or leave it uncontrolled, and it renders nothing itself.

parts.name: TooltipProvider
parts.description: Shares one delay between the tooltips below it, for example in a toolbar. The first opens after 600 ms, and moving to another trigger within 300 ms shows its tooltip at once.

parts.name: TooltipTrigger
parts.description: The element the tooltip describes. It opens on hover and keyboard focus, and you pass your Button or IconButton and turn off the description if the tooltip repeats the trigger's name.

parts.name: TooltipContent
parts.description: The dark surface, drawn in a portal above the trigger by default, 8 px away. Side, alignment and offset move it and it flips near a viewport edge, long text wraps at 240 or 320 px, Escape closes it.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The tooltip's text: one short phrase in 12 px medium, white.

parts.name: Shortcut
parts.description: A key hint in its own dark chip after the label. Write it for the platform: ⌘K on macOS, Ctrl+K on Windows.

parts.name: Arrow
parts.description: The small point towards the trigger, which you can hide. It turns with the side the tooltip ends up on and keeps pointing at the middle of the trigger.

items.text: Use it for a short hint on a control: the name of an icon button, a shortcut, a truncated text in full. For content people read at length or act on, use a Popover.
Give the trigger its own name with an aria-label, since a tooltip adds information and is never a control's only label. Turn off the description when it repeats that name.
Keep the text to one short phrase without a full stop. Longer text wraps at 240 px, or 320 px if allowed, and for more than three lines use a Popover.
Add a shortcut only if it works, and write it for the platform. Use the linger option for a confirmation like Copied to clipboard, which fades out slowly instead of snapping away.
Put a toolbar's tooltips in one TooltipProvider, so the delay is the same everywhere and moving along the buttons shows each tooltip at once.
Make the reason a control is disabled visible without hover, for example as helper text. The tooltip, on a wrapper that can take focus, then only repeats it.
Place the tooltip where it covers neither a neighbouring control nor the text of the row. Choose side and alignment for that, and let it flip near the edge.
Don't put links or buttons in a tooltip. It only opens on hover and focus of the trigger, so keyboard users can't reach them.
Don't make a tooltip the only place for an error, a confirmation or task-critical information. Touch and keyboard users may never see it.
Don't put a tooltip on text that isn't interactive. Nothing can take focus there, so a keyboard user never sees it.

useFor: The name of an icon button, with its shortcut
The full text of a label that is cut off with an ellipsis
A short hint on a control, or a confirmation that says what just happened

useInstead.name: Popover
useInstead.text: content people read at length or act on: more than three lines, links, buttons or a form

useInstead.name: Hover Card
useInstead.text: a preview of what a link points to, with an image or several lines of detail

useInstead.name: Alert
useInstead.text: an error, a warning or a message the user must see without hovering

keyboard.intro: A tooltip has no controls of its own. It follows the focus of its trigger, so you reach it with the keys that reach the trigger.

rows.action: Moves focus to the trigger. The tooltip opens as soon as the trigger receives keyboard focus, without the delay, and closes when focus leaves it.
Closes the open tooltip without moving focus. It opens again after the pointer or focus has left the trigger and returned.

keyboard.note: A tooltip is never focusable itself. A trigger that can't take focus, such as a disabled button, needs a focusable wrapper for the keyboard to reach its tooltip.

behavior.intro: What the tooltip does when it opens, where it goes, what it says and how it moves.

items.title: Opening
items.text: It opens when the pointer rests on the trigger for the delay, and at once on keyboard focus. It closes when pointer or focus leaves, on a press and on Escape, and touch has no hover.

items.title: Delay
items.text: By default the provider waits 600 ms and has a 300 ms timeout, so moving to the next trigger within it opens its tooltip at once. The docs site uses no delay, your app the default.

items.title: Placement
items.text: The tooltip sits on top by default, 8 px from the trigger. You choose the side and alignment, the arrow points at the trigger's middle, and near a viewport edge it flips and shifts back into view.

items.title: Width
items.text: The label grows to 240 px by default, or 320 px, then wraps and the surface grows taller. Padding is 16 px at the sides and 8 px above and below, 7 px when a shortcut chip is inside.

items.title: Surface
items.text: A dark surface with white text and a medium shadow, in light and dark theme alike. The corner is 8 px.

items.title: Shortcut
items.text: The shortcut is drawn in a dark chip after the label, 8 px away. The chip is a kbd element, so it is read as text.

items.title: Confirmation
items.text: The linger option opens the tooltip without the delay, and on close lets it drift up 4 px while it fades out slowly. Use it for a message that follows an action.

items.title: Accessibility
items.text: The surface has the tooltip role and an id. While it is open the trigger points at it with aria-describedby, unless you turn that off.

items.title: Motion
items.text: It opens with a quick fade and a zoom from 98 % after an 80 ms delay, so a passing pointer doesn't flash it, and closes faster. Within one group the animation is skipped.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the zoom and drift are off and the tooltip only fades.

minimalUsage.expected: A 36 px icon button. Hover it or focus it with Tab and a small dark tooltip with the text Copy link and a ⌘L chip appears above it.

Tooltip.open.description: Controls whether the tooltip is open. Pair it with `onOpenChange`; leave it out and the tooltip opens and closes on hover and focus by itself.

Tooltip.defaultOpen.description: Whether the tooltip is open on first render, when it is not controlled.

Tooltip.onOpenChange.description: Called when the tooltip should open or close, with the next value and the reason, such as the pointer, the focus or Escape.

Tooltip.disabled.description: Stops the tooltip from opening. The trigger keeps working as before.

Tooltip.trackCursorAxis.description: Makes the tooltip follow the pointer along an axis (`x`, `y` or `both`) instead of staying on the trigger. `none` is the default.

TooltipProvider.delay.description: How long, in milliseconds, the pointer must rest on a trigger before its tooltip opens. The default is 600. Keyboard focus is not delayed.

TooltipProvider.closeDelay.description: How long, in milliseconds, the tooltip stays open after the pointer has left. The default is 0.

TooltipProvider.timeout.description: The time, in milliseconds, after one tooltip closes during which moving to another trigger in the group opens its tooltip at once. The default is 300.

TooltipTrigger.render.description: Replaces the trigger's own element with your Button, IconButton or another element, which then gets the hover and focus behaviour and the `aria-describedby`.

TooltipTrigger.describe.description: Whether the trigger points to the open tooltip with `aria-describedby`. Set `false` when the tooltip only repeats the trigger's accessible name. The default is `true`.

TooltipTrigger.delay.description: Overrides the provider's delay for this trigger, in milliseconds.

TooltipTrigger.closeDelay.description: Overrides the provider's close delay for this trigger, in milliseconds.

TooltipTrigger.closeOnClick.description: Whether pressing the trigger closes the tooltip. The default is `true`.

TooltipTrigger.disabled.description: Stops this trigger from opening its tooltip. A natively disabled button cannot take focus; wrap it in an element with `tabIndex={0}` and make that the trigger.

TooltipContent.side.description: The side of the trigger the tooltip sits on: `top` (the default), `right`, `bottom` or `left`. It flips to the opposite side when there is no room.

TooltipContent.align.description: How the tooltip lines up with the trigger along the side: `start`, `center` (the default) or `end`. The arrow keeps pointing at the middle of the trigger.

TooltipContent.sideOffset.description: The distance between the trigger and the tooltip, in pixels. The default is 8.

TooltipContent.arrow.description: Shows the small point towards the trigger. Set `false` where the trigger is obvious. The default is `true`.

TooltipContent.shortcut.description: A key hint drawn in its own chip after the label, for example `⌘K`. Write it for the platform.

TooltipContent.maxWidth.description: The widest the label grows before the text wraps onto the next line: 240 px (the default) or 320 px for long translations.

TooltipContent.linger.description: For a confirmation such as `Copied to clipboard`: opens without the delay and, when it closes, drifts up slightly while it fades out slowly instead of snapping away.

TooltipContent.anchor.description: Positions the tooltip against another element or a virtual element instead of the trigger, for example the field a validation message belongs to.

TooltipContent.render.description: Replaces the surface's element with another element or component.

TooltipContent.className.description: Extra classes for the surface, merged after its own. A function receives the state and returns the classes.

TooltipContent.style.description: Inline styles for the surface. A function receives the state and returns the styles.

parts.name: Dialog
parts.description: Holds the open state and links the trigger to the window. Control it or leave it uncontrolled; it renders nothing itself.

parts.name: DialogTrigger
parts.description: The element that opens the dialog, usually a button. Focus returns to it when the dialog closes.

parts.name: DialogContent
parts.description: The window, with its own portal and overlay. It keeps focus inside, comes in three widths (384, 512 and 720 px) and can be non-modal and anchored to a corner.

parts.name: Close button
parts.description: The icon button in the top right corner, named Close for screen readers. It is on by default; turn it off only when the footer offers a clear way out.

parts.name: DialogHeader
parts.description: Stacks the progress, icon, title and description at the top, and leaves room for the close button.

parts.name: DialogProgress
parts.description: The step indicator of a short multi-step dialog (two to four steps), with an optional label for the current step. It is exposed as a progress bar.

parts.name: DialogIcon
parts.description: A round 40 px icon above the title in a default, warning or destructive look. Pass a Lucide icon as its child.

parts.name: DialogTitle
parts.description: Names the dialog, and screen readers announce it when the dialog opens. A title is needed even when the design shows none.

parts.name: DialogDescription
parts.description: One or two sentences on what the dialog is for, read out after the title.

parts.name: DialogBody
parts.description: The slot between header and footer for a form, a list or text. When scrollable, it scrolls between two rules while title and footer stay put, and keyboard users can focus it to scroll.

parts.name: DialogFooter
parts.description: The row of buttons, with the last one on the right and on top on a phone. It can paint a full-width band, stack the buttons, or put one action such as Back at the left edge.

parts.name: DialogClose
parts.description: Closes the dialog. Wrap the Cancel button in it, or turn on the footer's Close button.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: The primary Button, last in the footer. Name it after its result, such as Send invite, and show its pending state while the request runs.

parts.name: DialogOverlay
parts.description: The dimmed, lightly blurred backdrop. DialogContent already renders it, and a click on it closes the dialog.

parts.name: DialogPortal
parts.description: Moves the window to the end of the document. DialogContent already renders it, so you only need it for a custom window or container.

parts.name: DialogSurface
parts.description: The same window as a static panel without portal, overlay or focus trap, for previews and embedded layouts. Give it an aria-label.

items.text: Always include a DialogTitle, even when the design shows none. Without it the dialog has no name for screen readers.
Put the main action last and name it after its result: Send invite, Create project, not OK. Keep Cancel neutral next to it.
On a failed submit keep the dialog open and the input, and put the message on the field or in an Alert at the top of the body.
While the request runs, show the pending state on the primary action and disable the others. Close the dialog only after the server confirms.
Put long content in a scrollable DialogBody so the title and footer stay in view.
Don't confirm a destructive action in a Dialog, since a click outside closes it. An Alert Dialog closes only through a button or Escape.
Don't use a dialog to report that something worked. A saved state is a toast, and a dialog that needs a click to dismiss only adds a step.
Don't discard unsaved input silently when the dialog closes. Ask with an Alert Dialog on top, where Keep editing returns to the form.
Don't nest dialogs or use one for a long flow. More than four steps belong on a page.

useFor: A short task that needs full attention and ends with a decision, such as renaming a project or inviting a member
A small form, a choice from a list or a read-only summary before a user carries on
A short flow of two to four steps, such as creating a workspace

useInstead.name: Alert Dialog
useInstead.text: confirming an action that deletes data or removes access

useInstead.name: Sheet
useInstead.text: a long form or a detail view that needs more room

useInstead.name: Popover
useInstead.text: small content anchored to a control, without blocking the page

keyboard.intro: The buttons are native buttons, so the browser provides focus and activation. While a modal dialog is open the page behind it is inert.

rows.action: Moves focus between the close button, the fields and the buttons. In a modal dialog focus stays inside, wrapping from the last element to the first.
Presses the focused button. In a text field, Enter submits only when the field sits in a form.
Closes the dialog. A click on the backdrop closes it too, unless `disablePointerDismissal` is set.

behavior.intro: What the dialog does with focus, state, content and motion.

items.title: Modal
items.text: While a modal dialog is open, the page behind it is inert and does not scroll. The window is a dialog named by its title and described by its description.

items.title: Focus
items.text: Focus moves to the first focusable element when the dialog opens, or to one you choose. When it closes, focus returns to the trigger, or to a place you set.

items.title: Closing
items.text: The close button, a Close wrapped footer button, Escape and a click on the backdrop all close it. You can ignore the backdrop, for example while a request runs.

items.title: Non-modal
items.text: A non-modal dialog has no backdrop and no focus trap, so the page stays usable. Anchor it to the bottom right for help and side tasks.

items.title: Appearance
items.text: The surface look is the default: a semibold title, a footer band and a shadow. The plain look is the earlier flat one with a lighter title, no band and no shadow.

items.title: Scrolling
items.text: Long content goes into a scrollable body that scrolls up to 296 px between two rules while title and footer stay in view. Give it an aria-label so it is announced as a region.

items.title: Small screens
items.text: Below the small breakpoint the dialog fills the width minus 16 px gutters and the size setting has no effect. The footer stacks with the main action on top.

items.title: Previews in these docs
items.text: The window is portalled to the end of the document and fixed to the screen. The previews here draw it inside the card with the same behaviour, so it does not cover the page.

items.title: Opening and closing
items.text: The window fades in and zooms from 92% while sliding up 8 px, and the backdrop fades. Closing is a step faster and zooms down to 96%.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the zoom and slide are off and the window only fades, in and out.

parts.name: AlertDialog
parts.description: Holds the open state. Control it yourself, or leave it uncontrolled and let the trigger and buttons handle it.

parts.name: AlertDialogTrigger
parts.description: The element that opens the window, usually the button that starts the action. Focus returns to it when the window closes.

parts.name: AlertDialogContent
parts.description: The window, with its own portal and backdrop. It has no corner close button, so the footer buttons are the way out; the large size matches the 440 px Figma set.

parts.name: AlertDialogHeader
parts.description: Stacks the icon, the title and the description at the top of the window.

parts.name: AlertDialogIcon
parts.description: A 40 px tile with the icon above the title, in a default, warning or destructive tint. Without children it shows an alert circle, a warning triangle or a trash can.

parts.name: AlertDialogTitle
parts.description: Names the action and its object, like Delete project Northstar? It is the accessible name of the window.

parts.name: AlertDialogDescription
parts.description: Says what will be lost or cannot be undone. It is read out after the title.

parts.name: AlertDialogFeedback
parts.description: An announced message above the actions, as an error or warning: what failed, whether anything changed, what to do next.

parts.name: AlertDialogFooter
parts.description: The row of buttons. The last button in the markup sits on the right, or on top when the footer is stacked.

parts.name: AlertDialogCancel
parts.description: Closes the window without acting. Label it with the safe choice, such as Cancel or Keep editing.

parts.name: AlertDialogAction
parts.description: Confirms and closes on click. Primary by default, destructive for removals, or secondary for a third way out such as Discard changes.

parts.name: AlertDialogOverlay
parts.description: The dimmed, lightly blurred backdrop, already rendered by the content. Clicking it does nothing.

parts.name: AlertDialogPortal
parts.description: Moves the window to the end of the document. The content already uses it; you only need it for a custom window or container.

items.text: Name the object and the loss in the title, like Delete project Northstar, and put what goes with it in the description. Don't just ask Are you sure.
Repeat the action on the confirm button and make it destructive for deletions: Delete project after Cancel, so it ends up on the right.
Label the safe choice with what it does, like Keep editing or Cancel. When the action is hard to undo, focus starts on it.
For slow or failing actions, control the open state yourself. The action button closes the window on click, so prevent that, show the failure in the feedback area and turn the button into Retry.
Ask for a typed confirmation only for large deletions that cannot be undone, with a visible label, and never together with an acknowledgement.
Don't confirm with window.confirm. It cannot be styled or tested, while an Alert Dialog keeps the product's look, focus handling and button labels.
Don't use an Alert Dialog for a form or to report that something worked. A task with fields belongs in a Dialog, and success in a toast.
Don't ask for confirmation on routine actions that can be undone. Do them and offer Undo; a window for everything teaches people to click through.
Don't rely on a click outside or a corner close button to dismiss it. Neither exists here: the footer buttons and Escape are the way out.

useFor: Confirming an action that deletes data or removes access, such as deleting a project
Leaving a screen with unsaved changes
A consequence that needs one clear decision before it happens

useInstead.name: Toast
useInstead.text: saying that something worked, without asking for anything

useInstead.name: Alert
useInstead.text: a message that stays on the page

rows.action: Moves focus between the buttons and fields in the window. Focus stays inside it, wrapping from the last element to the first.
Presses the focused button: `AlertDialogAction` confirms and closes, `AlertDialogCancel` closes. In a text field, Enter does not confirm.
Closes the window without confirming, like Cancel. A click on the backdrop does nothing.

behavior.intro: What the window does with focus, state, content and motion.

items.title: Modal
items.text: While the window is open, the page behind it is inert and does not scroll. The window is an alert dialog named by its title and described by its description; give every window both.

items.title: No outside dismissal
items.text: A click on the backdrop never closes or confirms. Only a footer button or Escape does, so the decision is always explicit.

items.title: Focus
items.text: On open, focus moves to the first focusable element: the Cancel button, or the field if there is one (you can choose another). On close it returns to the trigger unless you send it elsewhere.

items.title: Closing and slow actions
items.text: Both the action and cancel buttons close the window on click. For a request that can fail, control the open state, keep the window open while it runs and close it on success.

items.title: Long text
items.text: The window has one shrinkable column, so a long title or file name wraps instead of widening it. With long action labels, stack the footer.

items.title: Footer layout
items.text: By default the footer stacks below the small breakpoint with the main action on top, and sits in a row above it. You can force either layout.

items.title: Previews in these docs
items.text: The window is portalled to the end of the document and fixed to the screen. The previews here draw the same window inside the card so it does not cover the page.

items.title: Opening and closing
items.text: The window fades in, zooms from 92 % and slides up 8 px; the backdrop fades. Closing is one step faster and zooms down to 96 %.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion on, zoom and slide are off and the window only fades in and out.

import {
  AlertDialog,
  AlertDialogAction,
  AlertDialogCancel,
  AlertDialogContent,
  AlertDialogDescription,
  AlertDialogFooter,
  AlertDialogHeader,
  AlertDialogIcon,
  AlertDialogTitle,
  AlertDialogTrigger,
} from "@/components/ui/alert-dialog"
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button"

export function DeleteProject() {
  return (
    <AlertDialog>
      <AlertDialogTrigger render={<Button variant="destructive" />}>Delete project</AlertDialogTrigger>
      <AlertDialogContent size="lg">
        <AlertDialogHeader>
          <AlertDialogIcon variant="destructive" />
          <AlertDialogTitle>Delete project “Northstar”?</AlertDialogTitle>
          <AlertDialogDescription>The project, its 24 tasks and all files will be permanently deleted. This can’t be undone.</AlertDialogDescription>
        </AlertDialogHeader>
        <AlertDialogFooter layout="inline">
          <AlertDialogCancel>Cancel</AlertDialogCancel>
          <AlertDialogAction variant="destructive">Delete project</AlertDialogAction>
        </AlertDialogFooter>
      </AlertDialogContent>
    </AlertDialog>
  )
}

parts.name: Collapsible
parts.description: Holds the open state and wraps the trigger and the panel. Appearance is row (a full-width trigger) or inline (a link-style trigger), and without it the trigger keeps the plus and minus box.

parts.name: CollapsibleTrigger
parts.description: The header, a button that reports whether it is expanded. It can show a leading icon, a second line, a summary while closed, a count badge and an indicator, and hover and press change its fill.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: The optional icon before the label. It is decorative and takes the text colour.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The children of the trigger. Name it after what is hidden, since it is the accessible name of the button and stays the same when the panel opens.

parts.name: Count
parts.description: The count badge after the label. It must equal the number of rows in the panel.

parts.name: Indicator
parts.description: The chevron that flips when the panel opens, or the plus and minus box. The default is the chevron in both appearances.

parts.name: CollapsibleRow
parts.description: Puts a control beside the trigger, never inside it. The action slot takes a button such as Edit.

parts.name: CollapsibleContent
parts.description: The panel. It opens on a grid-row transition, so nothing is measured, and sits 24 px below the trigger (16 px when nested), lined up with the trigger text.

parts.name: CollapsibleFeedback
parts.description: The loading, empty and error content of a panel, with an optional action such as Retry.

items.text: Pick row for a section header and inline for a link-style trigger under running text. Use one appearance per group of triggers.
Name the trigger after what is hidden, like Advanced options or Shipping details. Keep the title the same when it opens, and let only the indicator change.
Use the summary for what people need while the panel is closed, like 3 items and the total, and the count for the number of things inside. The count must equal the rows in the panel.
Keep fields a form needs outside the closed panel. A collapsed panel is easy to skip, and an error inside it stays out of sight.
Show loading, empty and error content with CollapsibleFeedback and offer an action such as Retry.
Don't put buttons or links inside CollapsibleTrigger, which is a button itself. Put an action beside it with CollapsibleRow.
Don't nest more than one level. For deeper structures use a tree view or separate pages.
Don't add a height transition to CollapsibleContent. It already animates with motion tokens, and a second animation fights it.
Don't stack several collapsibles to build an FAQ or a settings list. That is an Accordion, which also closes the open row.

useFor: One optional block that people open on demand, such as advanced options or a long description
A short summary that opens into its details, such as an order summary in a checkout
A link-style disclosure under running text, such as shipping details

useInstead.name: Accordion
useInstead.text: a list of several sections, such as an FAQ or grouped settings

useInstead.name: Tabs
useInstead.text: peer views of one object that people switch between

useInstead.name: Dialog
useInstead.text: a task that must block the page until it is done

keyboard.intro: The trigger is a native button, so the browser handles focus and activation.

rows.action: Moves focus to the next or previous trigger, and to a control placed beside it with `CollapsibleRow`.
Opens or closes the panel of the focused trigger.

behavior.intro: What the collapsible does with state, content, the DOM and motion.

items.title: Disabled
items.text: Disabling the Collapsible dims the trigger to 40 % and stops it from toggling.

items.title: Closed panels are not in the DOM
items.text: A closed panel is not rendered by default, so its text is missing from the server HTML and page search, and form values inside it are lost on close. Keep it mounted, or let find-in-page open it.

items.title: Always set the look
items.text: Appearance is optional. Without it the trigger keeps the legacy look, a bare label with the plus and minus box, and ignores icon, description, summary and count, so set it in new code.

items.title: Summary and count
items.text: The summary shows only while the panel is closed and hides when it opens, so use it for what people need before they open it. The count stays visible and must equal the rows inside.

items.title: Controls beside the trigger
items.text: A trigger is a button and cannot hold another button. CollapsibleRow puts an action next to it, and the action has its own focus stop.

items.title: Nesting
items.text: One collapsible can sit inside the panel of another, and its panel then opens 16 px below its trigger. Do not nest further.

items.title: Opening and closing
items.text: The panel follows the height of its content on a grid-row transition, without measuring it. The chevron turns 180 degrees.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the panel opens and closes instantly and the chevron flips without turning. The colour changes of hover and pressed stay.

minimalUsage.expected: You see a row with Order details and a chevron. The panel is open, and a click on the row closes it.

items.text: Give an icon-only Toggle an aria-label such as Bold. The pressed attribute announces the state, not the label.
Keep the label and icon the same in both states. A label that flips between Mute and Unmute makes a screen reader say the opposite of what the fill shows.

behavior.intro: What the toggle does with state, naming, looks, sizes and motion.

items.title: Pressed state
items.text: A toggle holds one boolean. Give it a default to start, or control it with a pressed value and change handler, and the state is exposed as aria-pressed.

items.title: Naming
items.text: A toggle is named by its text. An icon-only toggle has none so it needs an aria-label, and the name stays the same in both states.

items.title: Looks
items.text: Off is a white fill with a control border, light on hover and subtle while pressed. On is the indigo tint with its border and text, and the indigo tone is tinted at rest and solid while pressed.

items.title: Sizes
items.text: Five fixed heights: 32, 36, 40, 44 and 48 px, which don't follow density. The icon is 16 px at every size, and the label is 14 px up to large, 16 px at xl and 18 px at 2xl.

items.title: Disabled
items.text: A disabled toggle is a real disabled button. It keeps its state, drops to 40 % opacity, ignores the pointer and is skipped by Tab.

items.title: Focus
items.text: Keyboard focus draws the shared focus ring: an indigo border with a 2 px ring directly on the border.

items.title: Motion
items.text: Colours fade quickly. Nothing moves.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: There is no movement to remove, so reduced motion changes nothing. The colour change stays.

Keep one size per list, so the labels beside the tiles share one edge.

items.title: Tone in light and dark

items.title: Corners

items.title: Motion and reduced motion

parts.name: Meter
parts.description: The root: a div with the meter role and its minimum, maximum and current value. Children such as the label and value render above the bar.

parts.name: MeterLabel
parts.description: Names what is measured. Without a label, give Meter an aria-label.

parts.name: MeterValue
parts.description: Prints the formatted value at the right, a percent of the range by default, in tabular figures. It is hidden from assistive technology because the meter already announces its value.

parts.name: MeterIndicator
parts.description: The fill in the brand colour. It glides to a new value over the ambient duration, and Meter already renders it.

parts.name: MeterTrack
parts.description: The grey bar behind the fill, 8 px high and fully rounded. Meter renders it; you need it only for a custom layout.

items.text: Use a Meter for a measured value inside a known range: storage used, a score, a quota. For a task that runs to completion, use Progress.
Name it with MeterLabel or aria-label. Screen readers announce the value, and without a name they cannot say what it measures.
Set max to the real limit and show the unit: 38 of 50 GB, not a bare 76%. Use the format option or your own text in MeterValue.
When you print your own text, also pass getAriaValueText so a screen reader hears the same words: 38 of 50 gigabytes. Otherwise it announces the percent.
Measure bars that belong together against the same max, as in a storage widget, so the fills can be compared.
Say in words what a full or nearly full meter means and what to do: All seats are in use.
Don't use Meter for task progress. A meter reads as a measurement, so a half-full upload would look like a fixed value: use Progress.
Don't expect the fill to change colour near the limit. Meter has no low, high or optimum ranges, so tell the person in the text.
Don't animate the fill width yourself. It already moves with a transform, which is cheaper and matches the other bars.

useFor: A measured value inside a known range, such as storage used or seats in use
A score or a quota that is read against its limit
Several bars that share one limit and are compared with each other

useInstead.name: Progress

useInstead.name: Slider
useInstead.text: a value the person sets, not one that is shown

useInstead.name: Skeleton
