behavior.intro: What the meter does itself, and what it leaves to the page.

items.title: Role and value
items.text: Meter has the meter role with a minimum (0 by default), a maximum (100 by default) and the current value, clamped to that range. Its value text is a percent by default; a custom function replaces it.

items.title: Accessible name
items.text: The meter has no name of its own. A MeterLabel inside it becomes the name, or pass aria-label; MeterValue is hidden from assistive technology, so it is never the name.

items.title: Always a value
items.text: A meter measures something that exists, so the value is always a number. For a wait of unknown length use Progress with no value, or a Spinner.

items.title: No states
items.text: A meter has one size and one tone: an 8 px rounded track with a brand-colour fill. It looks the same when full and has no disabled or error look, so say that in text.

items.title: Format
items.text: Without a format the value prints as a percent: 38 of 50 prints 76%. With a format the value itself prints, for example 38 GB, and MeterValue children can be a function of the formatted and raw value.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The fill glides to a new value over 700 ms, moving only its transform. The first render draws it at its value without moving.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the fill jumps to its new value. Colour changes stay.

components.title: Kbd
components.description: Displays a keyboard key or shortcut, e.g. inside a search input.

parts.name: Kbd
parts.description: One key chip, 22 px high with a subtle fill, a border and a 4 px corner, holding a single key or a short symbol group like ⌘K. The inverse tone is a dark 18 px chip for surfaces like tooltips.

parts.name: KbdGroup
parts.description: Lines up several keys in a row with a 4 px gap. Its tone passes on to every direct Kbd child that has none of its own, and the separator is drawn between two keys.

parts.name: Separator
parts.description: The text between two keys: a plus for a combination, a word such as then for a sequence. It is muted on light surfaces, white on inverse, and absent after the last key.

parts.name: KbdHint
parts.description: The shortcut hint: key caps with a short label after them, for the foot of a command menu or next to a search field. The caps are 22 px high with a muted fill and 11 px text, the label is tertiary text. It replaces KeyboardHint.

items.text: Use Kbd to show a keyboard shortcut next to the action it triggers: in a menu item, a command palette, a tooltip, a search field or a shortcuts panel.
Put one key in each Kbd and join keys with KbdGroup. Use a plus separator when the keys read as one combination, such as Ctrl + Shift + P, and a word like then for a sequence.
Write the keys the way the platform labels them: ⌘, ⇧ and ⌥ on macOS, Ctrl, Shift and Alt on Windows. Keep one platform per list.
Use the inverse tone when the shortcut sits on a dark surface, and set it on the KbdGroup so every key follows. A Kbd wrapped in another element doesn't get the group's tone.
Set aria-keyshortcuts on the control the shortcut triggers. The chip is text for the eye; the attribute tells assistive technology.
Don't use Kbd for decoration or for text that is not a key. It is a hint, not a button, and it doesn't run the shortcut.
Don't list a shortcut that the app doesn't handle. A hint that does nothing erodes trust in every other hint.
Don't mix platforms in one list, such as ⌘S next to Ctrl+F. Read the platform and show one set.

useFor: The shortcut of an action, shown beside its label in a menu, a command palette or a shortcuts panel
A key hint inside a search field or a button, such as / or ⌘K
A combination or a sequence of keys in help text and documentation

useInstead.name: Tooltip
useInstead.text: a short label on hover or focus, which draws its own shortcut chip

useInstead.name: Dropdown Menu
useInstead.text: the shortcut of a menu item, which has its own DropdownMenuShortcut part

useInstead.name: Badge
useInstead.text: a status, a count or a label that is not a key

behavior.intro: What the chip does with its content, its group, its tone and motion.

items.title: Element
items.text: Kbd renders a native kbd element and KbdGroup a div. Neither is focusable or interactive, and screen readers read a chip as plain text.

items.title: Size
items.text: The default chip is 22 px high with a 20 px minimum width and 6 px side padding, in 12 px medium text. The inverse chip is 18 px high with an 18 px minimum width and 5 px padding, in 12 px semibold.

items.title: Grouping
items.text: KbdGroup is an inline flex row with a 4 px gap. The separator sits between two keys, never after the last one, and a group with neither tone nor separator just lines the keys up.

items.title: Tone
items.text: The group's tone is applied to each direct Kbd child that has none of its own, so one prop turns a whole combination inverse. The separator turns white with it.

items.title: Theme
items.text: The default chip uses the subtle, border and secondary text tokens; the inverse chip uses the tooltip key token and white. Both follow the theme and dark mode with no extra class.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The chip has no state and no transition. Nothing in it moves.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: There is no animation to reduce, so reduced motion changes nothing.

minimalUsage.expected: You see the text Open the command palette followed by two 22 px key chips, Ctrl and K, with a + between them.

Kbd.tone.description: `default` is the light 22 px chip with a border, for pages and cards. `inverse` is the dark 18 px chip with white text, for dark surfaces such as a tooltip.

KbdGroup.separator.description: What is drawn between two keys: a plus, a word such as `then`, or any node. Nothing is drawn after the last key. Leave it out to line the keys up with only the 4 px gap.

KbdGroup.tone.description: Passed on to every direct `Kbd` child that has no tone of its own, and sets the colour of the separator. A `Kbd` inside another element does not receive it.

KbdHint.keys.description: The key caps, one string each, such as `["⌘", "K"]` or `["Esc"]`. Required.

KbdHint.label.description: The short text after the keys, such as `to search` or `to close`. Required.

KbdHint.className.description: Extra classes on the hint, for example to change the gap to the next hint.

components.title: Spinner
components.description: A spinning indicator for an in-progress loading state.
components.props: function Spinner({ className, ...props }: React.ComponentProps<"svg">): React.JSX.Element;

parts.name: Spinner
parts.description: A Lucide loader icon that turns once a second, 16 px and muted by default, announced as Loading. Pass an aria-label to say what is loading, or hide it when a visible text already does.

items.text: Use it for a short wait tied to an action: a status line that saves, a panel that refreshes. When content with a known layout loads, use a Skeleton.
When the spinner stands alone, pass a specific aria-label such as Saving changes. The default Loading says nothing about what is happening.
Beside a visible text, hide the spinner from screen readers and make the text a status, so the change is announced once, not twice.
Match the size to its neighbours: 16 px for body text, 24 px for a row icon, 32 px for a panel. Use the primary colour for a wait the person started, and keep the muted default for background work.
Keep the space the spinner takes when it goes away, so the layout doesn't move. Give its row a fixed height or swap in an icon of the same size.
Don't put a Spinner inside a Button. A button has a pending state that draws the spinner, keeps its width and blocks a second press.
Don't swap a chart or list for a Spinner while it loads, because the area collapses and the layout jumps. Use a Skeleton of the same size.
Don't use a Spinner when you know how far along the task is. Show a Progress bar, so people can tell whether it is worth waiting.

useFor: A short wait on an action, such as saving, syncing or refreshing, where the length is not known
A status line or a row that shows a job is running
A panel with no layout to show yet, such as a dashboard that is loading its first data

useInstead.name: Skeleton
useInstead.text: content with a known layout that loads, such as a table, a list or a card

useInstead.name: Progress
useInstead.text: a task that reports how far it has come, such as an upload

useInstead.name: Button
useInstead.text: the wait after pressing a button, since its pending state draws the spinner for you

behavior.intro: What the spinner does with size, colour, motion and assistive technology.

items.title: Size
items.text: The icon is 16 px by default. Set another size with a class such as 24 or 32 px, which wins because it is applied after the default.

items.title: Colour
items.text: The icon is muted by default. Set the brand colour or any other text colour, and the stroke follows it, so there is one colour and no fill.

items.title: Accessibility
items.text: The icon is a status labelled Loading, which is announced politely when it appears. Pass an aria-label for a specific name, or hide it when a text beside it says what is loading.

items.title: Layout
items.text: The icon takes its size from the class and nothing else: no margin, no label, no container. Place it in a flex row with a small gap beside a text.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The icon turns once a second without end. It only rotates, through a transform.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the icon does not turn. It stays on screen as a still loader and keeps its status role, so the state is still announced.

minimalUsage.expected: You see a small grey loader icon turning beside the text Saving changes.

parts.name: Toolbar
parts.description: A framed row with the toolbar role, a 1 px border, the card fill and a 12 px corner, with 4 px of padding and gaps. It is one tab stop with arrow keys between items, named with an aria-label.

parts.name: ToolbarGroup
parts.description: Keeps related buttons close together with a 2 px gap, such as the text styles. It has the group role, and disabling it disables every item inside.

parts.name: ToolbarButton
parts.description: A 32 px square button with an 8 px corner for one icon. It joins the roving focus, and becomes a toggle when you render it as one: a pressed one takes the indigo tint.

parts.name: ToolbarSeparator
parts.description: A 1 px line between two groups, 20 px long with 4 px of margin on each side. It runs across the toolbar, vertical in a horizontal one and horizontal in a vertical one.

parts.name: ToolbarLink
parts.description: A 14 px text link in the toolbar that arrow keys reach like the buttons. Use it for a destination such as a help page, and a button for an action.

items.text: Use it for controls that act on one thing, such as the formatting buttons of an editor or the tools of a canvas. For joined buttons that switch a view, use a Button Group.
Name the toolbar with an aria-label, such as Text formatting, and give every icon-only button its own aria-label.
Sort buttons into groups with a separator between them, so related actions sit together and arrow keys still pass through the whole row.
Show a tooltip with the name and shortcut on every icon button, and wrap one toolbar's tooltips in one TooltipProvider so they share a delay.
Keep a toolbar to one row of 4 to 12 items. When you need more tools, move the least used behind an overflow button instead of letting the row scroll.
Don't add your own arrow-key handling or tabIndex to the items. The toolbar already moves focus between them, and Tab leaves it.
Don't swap a button for a menu, select or field without testing it with the keyboard. Only buttons, links and inputs of the toolbar take part in its roving focus.
Don't use a Toolbar to navigate between pages. Use tabs or a navigation bar, since a toolbar is for actions on the thing in front of the user.

useFor: The formatting buttons above an editor, the tools of a canvas or the actions of a selection
A row of icon buttons that should be one tab stop with arrow-key movement
Toggles that switch a style on or off, alone or as one of a set

useInstead.name: Button Group
useInstead.text: joined buttons that belong together, such as a view switch or a split action

useInstead.name: Action Bar
useInstead.text: the actions that appear for a selection of rows, with a count and a way to clear it

useInstead.name: Icon Button
useInstead.text: a single icon action that stands on its own, not in a row of actions

keyboard.intro: The toolbar is built on the Base UI toolbar. It keeps one item in the tab order and moves focus between the items with arrow keys.

rows.action: Moves focus into the toolbar, onto the item that last had focus (the first one at the start), and out of it again. The toolbar is one tab stop however many items it holds.
Moves focus to the previous or next item in a horizontal toolbar. From the last item it wraps to the first, unless `loopFocus` is `false`.
Does the same in a vertical toolbar (`orientation="vertical"`). The keys of the other axis do nothing.
Presses the focused button. On a toggle it switches it on or off. On a ToolbarLink, Enter follows the link.

keyboard.note: Disabled buttons stay reachable with arrow keys because they remain focusable by default. Turn that off on a button to skip it.

behavior.intro: What the toolbar does with focus, state, layout and motion.

items.title: Role and name
items.text: The root has the toolbar role and an orientation. Give it an aria-label so a screen reader announces what it is, and a group has the group role.

items.title: Focus
items.text: Focus is roving: one item is in the tab order and arrow keys move it. The focused item draws a 2 px indigo ring on its edge, which fits in the 4 px padding and is not clipped.

items.title: Pressed
items.text: A ToolbarButton is a plain button, and rendering it as a Toggle makes it report pressed. The pressed button takes the indigo tint, border and text, and keeps the tint on hover.

items.title: Disabled
items.text: A disabled item or toolbar is announced as disabled, drawn at 40 % opacity and ignores the pointer. It stays in the arrow-key order unless you turn that off.

items.title: Orientation
items.text: Vertical orientation only changes the arrow keys and the announced orientation. The layout stays a row until you stack the toolbar and groups, and the separator then needs a horizontal line style.

items.title: Concentric corners
items.text: The 8 px button corner sits 4 px inside the 12 px toolbar corner. A toolbar with larger buttons and more padding needs a larger corner, for example 16 px for 8 px of padding.

items.title: Theme
items.text: The frame uses the card and border tokens, and buttons use secondary text with page and subtle fills for hover and pressed. They follow the theme and dark mode with no extra class.

items.title: Motion
items.text: A button fades its colour on hover and press. Only colour animates, and nothing moves or resizes.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: Nothing moves, so there is no animation to remove. The colour change is the same with reduced motion.

}

parts.name: DropdownMenu
parts.description: Holds the open state and links the trigger to the menu. Control it or leave it uncontrolled; it renders nothing itself.

parts.name: DropdownMenuTrigger
parts.description: The element that opens the menu, usually a button. It opens on click, Enter, Space or Arrow Down and reports that it has a popup and whether it is expanded.

parts.name: DropdownMenuContent
parts.description: The menu, with its own portal and positioner. It is as wide as its longest entry (8 to 20 rem), never taller than the room left, and hides when its trigger scrolls out of view.

parts.name: DropdownMenuGroup
parts.description: Groups related entries. A label inside it becomes the accessible name of the group.

parts.name: DropdownMenuLabel
parts.description: A heading for a group of entries. Inside a group it names the group, on its own it is a plain heading, and it is not an entry, so arrow keys skip it.

parts.name: DropdownMenuItem
parts.description: An action that runs on click and closes the menu, with an optional icon, avatar, description or red destructive look. A disabled entry stays focusable so people can find it.

parts.name: DropdownMenuShortcut
parts.description: The visible shortcut hint at the right of an entry. It is hidden from screen readers, so put the binding on the entry itself.

parts.name: DropdownMenuSub
parts.description: Holds the open state of one submenu. It renders nothing itself.

parts.name: DropdownMenuSubTrigger
parts.description: The entry that opens a submenu, with a chevron at the right. It opens on hover after 100 ms, with Arrow Right or with Enter.

parts.name: DropdownMenuSubContent
parts.description: The submenu, flush against its entry on the side the text ends. It is smaller, so it opens a step faster than the main menu.

parts.name: DropdownMenuCheckboxItem
parts.description: An entry that toggles an option, with a check at the right. An indeterminate state shows a dash for a select-all entry, and the menu can stay open while people toggle.

parts.name: DropdownMenuRadioGroup
parts.description: Holds the chosen value of a set of radio entries and reports a change.

parts.name: DropdownMenuRadioItem
parts.description: One choice of a radio group, with a check at the right while it is chosen.

parts.name: DropdownMenuSeparator
parts.description: A one pixel rule between two sets of entries. Put the destructive entry after one.

parts.name: DropdownMenuLoading
parts.description: A status line with a spinner for entries that are still loading. It is not an entry, so arrow keys skip it, and the content should be marked busy while it shows.

parts.name: DropdownMenuEmpty
parts.description: A centred line for a menu with nothing to show, so it never opens as an empty box.

parts.name: DropdownMenuPortal
parts.description: Moves the menu to the end of the document. The content already renders it, so you only need it for a custom container.

items.text: Name destructive entries after the action and the object, and use the destructive variant: Delete project, not Delete. The colour is a second cue, never the only one.
Put the destructive entry last, after a separator, and the most used entries first.
Disable an entry that does not apply right now instead of removing it. Arrow keys still reach it, so screen reader users learn that the action exists.
Show a loading line while entries load and an empty line when there are none, with the content marked busy while loading. The menu never opens as an empty box.
Put the shortcut in the shortcut part and the binding in aria-keyshortcuts, so a screen reader says Copy without reading out the keys.
Don't put links to pages in a Dropdown Menu. It is a menu of actions; navigation belongs in the navbar menu or in plain links.
Don't use it to pick a value for a form field. A Select or a Combobox shows the chosen value in the field itself.
Don't pile up entries. Past seven or eight, split the menu into labelled groups, and never nest more than one submenu.

useFor: A short list of actions behind a button, such as rename, duplicate and delete on a row
Options that toggle or choose without leaving the page, such as view settings and sort order
The account menu behind an avatar

useInstead.name: Select
useInstead.text: picking one value for a form field

useInstead.name: Context Menu
useInstead.text: actions on a right click or a long press

useInstead.name: Popover
useInstead.text: content with controls of its own, not a list of actions

keyboard.intro: The trigger is a native button, so the browser provides focus and activation. Once the menu is open, focus is inside it and the arrow keys move between the entries.

rows.action: On the trigger: opens the menu and moves focus to its first entry. Arrow Up opens it and moves focus to the last entry.
Moves focus to the next or previous entry. Disabled entries are reached too, and focus wraps at the ends.
Moves focus to the first or the last entry.
Type-ahead: typing the start of a label moves focus to the next entry that begins with it.
Runs the focused entry and closes the menu. A checkbox or radio entry with `closeOnClick={false}` toggles and keeps the menu open.
On a submenu entry: opens the submenu and moves focus into it. Arrow Left closes it and returns to the entry. The directions swap in right-to-left layouts.
Closes the current level, the submenu first and then the menu, and returns focus to the trigger.
Closes the menu when focus leaves it.

behavior.intro: What the menu does with focus, state, content and motion.

items.title: Entries and activation
items.text: Entries are menu items, checkbox items or radio items. A click or Enter runs the entry and closes the menu, and checkbox and radio entries do the same unless you keep the menu open.

items.title: Disabled entries
items.text: A disabled entry is dimmed and cannot run, but it stays focusable and is announced as unavailable, as the WAI-ARIA menu pattern asks. Keyboard and screen reader users still see the action.

items.title: Focus
items.text: Focus moves into the menu when it opens and returns to the trigger when it closes. You can send it somewhere else on close.

items.title: Modal
items.text: A menu is modal by default: the page behind it is inert and does not scroll while it is open. You can turn that off to leave the page usable.

items.title: Position and size
items.text: The menu opens 4 px below the trigger, aligned to its start, and flips to the other side when there is no room. It is as wide as its longest entry and scrolls when the room runs out.

items.title: Submenus
items.text: A submenu opens on hover after 100 ms, and moving diagonally towards it does not close it. Arrow Right or Enter opens it at once, and in right-to-left layouts its side flips.

items.title: Selection
items.text: A checkbox entry reports its checked state, and an indeterminate one shows a dash and counts as mixed. A radio group reports the chosen value, and the check fades in instantly.

items.title: Previews in these docs
items.text: The menu is portalled to the end of the document and floats over the page. The previews here draw it inside the card and show it only while the whole card is on screen.

items.title: Opening and closing
items.text: The menu fades in and scales up from the trigger while sliding 4 px in from its side, and closes a step faster. A submenu opens faster too, and one opened with the keyboard skips the transition.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the transition is off and the menu appears and disappears at once.

minimalUsage.code:
import {
  DropdownMenu,
  DropdownMenuContent,
  DropdownMenuItem,
  DropdownMenuSeparator,
  DropdownMenuTrigger,
} from "@/components/ui/dropdown-menu"
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button"
import { ChevronDown } from "lucide-react"

export function ProjectActions() {
  return (
    <DropdownMenu>
      <DropdownMenuTrigger render={<Button variant="plain" />}>
        Options
        <ChevronDown data-icon="inline-end" />
      </DropdownMenuTrigger>
      <DropdownMenuContent>
        <DropdownMenuItem>Rename</DropdownMenuItem>
        <DropdownMenuItem>Duplicate</DropdownMenuItem>
        <DropdownMenuSeparator />
        <DropdownMenuItem variant="destructive">Delete project</DropdownMenuItem>
      </DropdownMenuContent>
    </DropdownMenu>
  )
}

items.title: Opening
items.text: The card opens 100 ms after the pointer enters the trigger or it gets keyboard focus. The underlying default of 600 ms feels as if the preview never loads, and you can change the delay.

items.title: Closing
items.text: The card closes 100 ms after the pointer leaves both the trigger and the card, so you can move onto the card and select text. Escape closes it at once.

items.title: Touch
items.text: Touch screens can't hover, so a tap follows the link. The preview is an extra: everything in it must also be on the page the link goes to.

items.title: Not a dialog
items.text: Focus never moves into the card and it isn't announced as a popup. Don't put anything in it that people must reach with the keyboard.

items.title: Position and size
items.text: The card opens below the trigger, centred, 8 px away and 288 px wide. Set the side to open it above or beside the trigger; it flips when there is no room.

items.text: With reduced motion the scale is off and the card only fades in and out.

items.text: Give the panel one clear job: a short form, a list of options, or a question with its buttons. Keep a title and a line of text so people know what they opened.
Set a width, such as 16 rem. Without one the panel is as wide as its widest line.
Wrap Cancel and Apply in the close part, so focus goes back to the trigger.
Put the trigger where people expect the content to belong, and align the panel so it stays inside the page at the screen edge.
Don't put a long form, a table or a multi-step task in a popover. Use a Dialog or a side panel when people need the room.
Don't use it for a short label on an icon. A Tooltip is for that, and it needs no click.
Don't open one popover from inside another. Move the second choice into the first panel.
Don't hide the only way to do something in a popover that opens on hover. Touch screens cannot hover, so keep the click.

Settings for one object, opened from a button on that object

keyboard.intro: The trigger is a native button, so the browser provides focus and activation. The panel is not a menu: its controls are reached with Tab.

rows.action: On the trigger: opens the panel and moves focus into it. On the trigger of an open panel: closes it.
Moves focus through the controls in the panel. Moving focus out of the panel closes it.
Closes the panel and gives the focus back to the trigger.

behavior.intro: What the panel does with focus, the page behind it and motion.

items.title: Opening
items.text: Clicking the trigger, or pressing Enter or Space on it, opens the panel and moves focus to the first control, or to the panel if it has none. You can choose which element gets focus.

items.title: Closing
items.text: Escape, a click outside, the close part, or moving focus out of the panel closes it. Focus goes back to the trigger unless you send it elsewhere.

items.title: The page behind
items.text: By default the page behind stays usable and scrolls, and a click on it closes the panel. Modal locks scroll and pointer outside; the trap-focus option only keeps focus inside.

items.title: Position and size
items.text: The panel opens below the trigger, centred, 8 px away, and you can pick another side and alignment. It flips when there is no room and slides to stay on screen.

items.title: Content that loads
items.text: Show a skeleton of the final layout while content loads, and a short line with the next step when it fails, so the panel never opens empty. Mark a loading panel as busy.

items.title: Previews in these docs
items.text: In these docs the previews draw the panel inside the preview and show it only while the whole preview is on screen. It starts open; click the trigger to close and reopen it.

items.title: Opening and closing
items.text: The panel fades in and scales up from 95 % with an overshoot curve, growing from the side of the trigger. It leaves with a fade and a scale down to 99 %.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the scale is off and the panel only fades in and out.

minimalUsage.expected: You should see a button named Pipeline. Pressing it opens a small panel under it with a title and a line of text; pressing Escape or clicking elsewhere closes it.

Popover.defaultOpen.description: Whether the panel starts open, for an uncontrolled popover. `false` by default.

Popover.onOpenChange.description: Called with the new open state whenever the panel opens or closes, with details about what caused it.

Popover.modal.description: `false` keeps the page behind the panel usable, `true` locks the scroll and the pointer outside the panel, and `"trap-focus"` only keeps the focus inside. `false` by default.

PopoverTrigger.render.description: Replaces the trigger element, usually with a `Button` or an `IconButton`, so the trigger looks like the rest of your buttons.

PopoverTrigger.openOnHover.description: Opens the panel when the pointer rests on the trigger as well as on click. Touch screens cannot hover, so keep the click working. `false` by default.

PopoverTrigger.delay.description: How long the pointer must rest on the trigger before the panel opens with `openOnHover`, in milliseconds.

PopoverTrigger.closeDelay.description: How long after the pointer has left the trigger and the panel the panel closes with `openOnHover`, in milliseconds.

PopoverContent.side.description: The side of the trigger the panel opens on: `top`, `right`, `bottom` or `left`. It flips to the other side when there is no room.

PopoverContent.align.description: How the panel lines up with the trigger along that side: `start`, `center` or `end`. `center` by default.

PopoverContent.sideOffset.description: The distance between the trigger and the panel in pixels. 8 by default.

PopoverContent.anchor.description: An element or a ref the panel is positioned against instead of the trigger.

PopoverContent.initialFocus.description: The element that gets the focus when the panel opens. By default the first control in the panel.

PopoverContent.finalFocus.description: The element that gets the focus when the panel closes. By default the trigger.

items.text: Name the table with a caption, or with an aria-label when the page heading already does. On a table that scrolls sideways, that name also labels the scroll region.
Right-align numbers, heading included, and use tabular figures so they line up and don't shift when they change. Text stays left.
Give amounts and quantities their unit. CurrencyCell adds the currency, and for other figures the column heading names the unit.
Show a missing value as an em dash and give screen readers the words No value. An empty cell looks like a mistake, and a 0 claims something the data doesn't.
Keep the header while the table loads, is empty or fails, and show the state where the rows go. The columns stay put, so nothing jumps when rows arrive.
Don't set row padding or heights by hand. Rows follow the density setting.
Don't make a row clickable when nothing inside it is. A row has no focus ring or key action, so put a link or button in the first cell.
Don't stack many columns on a phone. A sideways scroll hides the right-hand columns, so pick the few that matter or use a list.
Don't build sorting, filters or paging by hand around a Table. When people need them, use Data Table, which keeps that state for you.

useFor: Rows people read and compare: invoice line items, a list of members, usage per product
A short, fixed set of columns where every row has the same shape
A summary row that closes the table with a named total

useInstead.name: Data Table
useInstead.text: sorting, filters, bulk actions, column settings and server-side data

useInstead.name: List Group
useInstead.text: rows without columns, such as an activity list or a settings list

keyboard.intro: A table isn't a widget, so rows and cells take no focus and have no key commands. Keys work on the scroll region and on the controls in your cells.

rows.action: Moves focus to the next or previous control in a cell: a checkbox, a button, a link or a select. When the table is wider than its card, the scroll region is the first stop.
On the focused scroll region: scrolls the table sideways. ArrowUp and ArrowDown scroll it vertically when it has a fixed height.
Ticks or clears a focused checkbox, or picks a focused radio. The row turns subtle with it.
Presses a focused button, such as an icon action or the call to action of a row.

behavior.intro: What the table does with its rows, columns, width and motion.

items.title: Native table
items.text: Table renders a real table inside a scroll box, so screen readers announce rows, columns and headers. Headings are real th cells and the caption is a real caption.

items.title: Row colours
items.text: The header row has the page background. A row lightens on hover, a selected row stays subtle even on hover, and a row with an open menu keeps its hover colour.

items.title: Primary column
items.text: The first cell of a row is in the text colour and the others are secondary, so the eye lands on the name. A leading checkbox or expand button doesn't count, and you can mark another cell as primary.

items.title: Alignment
items.text: Text is left-aligned and numbers are right-aligned with tabular figures, in the cells and the heading above them. A column keeps one alignment from top to bottom.

items.title: Summary row
items.text: The footer closes the table with a line and medium weight. Its first cell names what the row adds up, and the figure sits right-aligned in its column.

items.title: Caption
items.text: The caption sits below the rows by default, and caption-top moves it above. When the page already names the table, hide the caption visually: it stays the accessible name.

items.title: Width
items.text: Cells don't wrap. A table wider than its container scrolls inside it and the scroll box takes focus, and you can let a text column wrap where you want.

items.title: Density
items.text: Header height and row padding follow the density setting. A one-line row is about 33 px by default, and comfortable density makes both larger.

items.title: Missing values
items.text: A value that doesn't exist is an em dash, never 0 and never an empty cell. Hide the dash from screen readers and give them the words No value.

items.title: Loading, empty and error
items.text: The table has no states of its own. Keep the header and put skeleton rows, an empty state or an error with a Retry button where the rows go, marked busy while loading.

items.title: Motion
items.text: Nothing moves. Rows change background on hover and selection, and icon actions change colour, all with short fades.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: There is no movement to remove, so reduced motion changes nothing. The short colour fades stay.

items.text: Write short labels in sentence case, one or two words: Billing history, not Billing History.
Keep every tab in a row the same kind: all labels, all icons with labels, or all with counts.
Always start with a selected tab. Keep the value in state or in the URL when people should be able to come back to a tab.
Give the list an aria-label, such as Project sections, when a page has more than one row of tabs.
Keep the number of tabs small enough for a phone. The row scrolls sideways when it runs out of room, and a tab past the edge is easy to miss.
Don't use tabs to move between pages. Links that change the route are navigation with aria-current, not a tab list.
Don't add your own key handlers to the tabs. Arrow keys, Home and End already move between them, and Tab moves on into the panel.
Don't set heights on the list or tabs. Pick a size instead, which follows the density and matches the Button sizes.
Don't hide what people must read or do in a tab they may never open. Put required information outside the tabs.

A settings page split into a few sections that people switch between
Views of one list with a count each, such as All, Open and Done
