DatePicker.typeable.description: Turns a `field` into a text box with a calendar button, so the date can be typed.

DatePicker.defaultText.description: The text a typeable field starts with, for example a draft that is not a date yet. It is checked on mount.

DatePicker.today.description: Overrides the date of today, which defaults to `new Date()`. Use it for demos and tests.

DatePicker.confirmation.description: `apply` (the default) keeps a draft until Apply; `instant` commits a single date on the click and leaves the footer out.

DatePicker.unit.description: `days` (the default) or `nights`: what the range length in the summary is counted in.

DatePicker.presets.description: Range only. `true` shows the eight built-in quick ranges at the left; an array of `{ label, range }` shows your own, where `range` gets `{ today, min }` and returns `{ from, to }`.

DatePicker.numberOfMonths.description: Range only. `1` or `2` months side by side. It defaults to 2, and to 1 for presets below 830 px.

DatePicker.open.description: Whether the popover is open, to control it.

DatePicker.defaultOpen.description: Whether the popover starts open when `open` is not set.

DatePicker.onOpenChange.description: Called with the new open state when the popover opens or closes.

DatePicker.placeholder.description: The text shown while empty. It defaults to `Pick a date` or `Pick a date range` for a button, and to the format for a field.

DatePicker.min.description: The earliest day that can be picked or typed.

DatePicker.max.description: The latest day that can be picked or typed.

DatePicker.disabled.description: Days that cannot be picked or typed: a list of dates, or a function that returns true for a blocked day.

DatePickerPanel.value.description: The date or range the draft starts from.

DatePickerPanel.onApply.description: Called with the draft when Apply is pressed, and in `instant` mode with the day that was clicked.

DatePickerPanel.presets.description: Range only. `true` or an array of presets, as on DatePicker.

DatePickerPanel.numberOfMonths.description: Range only. `1` or `2` months side by side. It defaults to 2.

DatePickerPanel.stacked.description: Stacks the two months of a range below each other, for a narrow container.

DatePickerPanel.min.description: The earliest day that can be picked.

DatePickerPanel.max.description: The latest day that can be picked.

DatePickerPanel.disabled.description: Days that cannot be picked: a list of dates, or a function.

DatePickerPanel.defaultMonth.description: The month the first calendar starts on. It defaults to the month of the draft, else today.

DatePickerPanel.unit.description: `days` or `nights`, for the length in the summary.

DatePickerPanel.error.description: An error message for the summary line. It keeps Apply off.

DatePickerPanel.surface.description: Draws a border, the popover surface and a shadow, for a panel that sits on the page.

DatePickerPanel.header.description: `label` or `month-year`, the header of the calendars.

DatePickerField.mode.description: `single` or `range`, which decides the placeholder and the helper line.

DatePickerField.value.description: The date or range to show.

DatePickerField.helperText.description: The line under the field; `false` hides it.

DatePickerField.error.description: An error message under the field.

DatePickerField.open.description: Draws the field as open, with its focus ring.

DatePickerField.id.description: The id the label and the value are tied to.

DatePickerFooter.summary.description: The text at the left: what is missing, an error or the choice.

DatePickerFooter.invalid.description: Draws the summary as an error.

DatePickerFooter.className.description: Extra classes for the footer row.

components.title: Alert
components.description: An inline banner in 5 colors and 2 sizes, with an optional close button and action.

props.name: icon
props.description: Replaces the leading icon (default: a check circle, a warning triangle for negative and warning; with `size="inline"` a shield check). `null` hides it.

parts.name: Alert
parts.description: The banner, with role alert. It comes in five variants (plain, positive, primary, negative, warning) and two sizes (large, small), and picks its icon from the variant. With size inline it is a static line of text without a box and without the role.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: The leading icon: a check circle, or a warning triangle for negative and warning. You can replace it or hide it.

parts.name: AlertTitle
parts.description: The bold first line. In the small size it stays on one line and truncates only when the banner is very narrow.

parts.name: AlertDescription
parts.description: The message. In large it wraps under the title; in small it takes the rest of the line and ends in an ellipsis.

parts.name: Close button
parts.description: A native button named Dismiss, drawn only when a close handler is set.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: Any Button after the description, usually plain and small. In large it sits under the text; in small it ends the row.

items.text: Say what happened in the title and what to do next in the text, like Changes couldn't be saved and Check your connection and try again.
Pick the colour for the meaning: positive for done, negative for failed, warning for attention, primary for information and plain for a neutral note.
Place the alert next to what it is about: under the field that failed, or at the top of the section it describes.
Give an alert that is only information a close button, and keep one that blocks people on the page until the cause is fixed.
Don't use an alert for a confirmation that should vanish by itself. A Toast fits a short message after an action.
Don't stack more than two or three alerts. Merge them into one, or move the details into a list.
Don't rely on the colour alone. The title and the text must say what happened, because not everyone sees the colour.
Don't put long text or a form in an alert. Link to a page for the details.

useFor: A message that belongs to the page or to one section and stays until the cause is fixed or the reader closes it
The result of a form or a bulk action, shown where people are looking
A notice at the top of a page, such as an ending trial or a planned maintenance window

useInstead.name: Toast
useInstead.text: a short confirmation that appears after an action and disappears by itself

useInstead.name: Alert Dialog
useInstead.text: a decision people must make before they can go on

useInstead.name: Empty State
useInstead.text: a list or a page that has nothing in it yet

keyboard.intro: The alert itself is not focusable. Only the action and the close button are in the tab order.

rows.action: Moves focus to the action and to the close button.
Presses the focused button: runs the action, or calls `onClose`.

behavior.intro: What the alert announces, how it is coloured and what it leaves to you.

items.title: Announcement
items.text: The alert is an assertive live region: a screen reader reads it as soon as it is added, and does not read one that was there at load. For a non-urgent message, use the polite status role.

items.title: Colour
items.text: A coloured alert has a tint fill with text, icon and border in the tint text colour of the same hue; plain uses the card colour. Every pair is a fixed token, so it works in light and dark.

items.title: Size
items.text: Large stacks title, text and action in a column. Small keeps them in one row, which fits above a table or at the top of a page; the text truncates there, so long messages belong in large.

items.title: Closing
items.text: Pressing the close button calls your handler; the alert does not remove itself. Stop rendering it yourself, and move focus somewhere sensible if the alert held it.

items.title: Width
items.text: The alert is a block that fills its container. Set the width on the container, not on the alert.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The alert has no entrance or exit animation. The close button sits at 70 % opacity and fades to 100 % on hover and focus.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion on nothing changes: the only motion is an opacity fade, which stays.

minimalUsage.expected: You should see a green banner with a check icon, a bold title and one line of text under it.

Alert.variant.description: The colour and meaning: `plain` for a neutral note, `positive` for success, `primary` for information, `negative` for an error and `warning` for attention. `plain` by default.

Alert.size.description: `large` stacks the title, the text and an action in a column; `small` keeps them in one row; `inline` drops the box for a 12 px line of text with a 14 px icon and no `role="alert"`. `large` by default.

Alert.icon.description: Replaces the leading icon. Without it the alert shows a check circle, or a warning triangle for `negative` and `warning`; with `size="inline"` a shield check, or the triangle for `warning`. `null` hides it.

Alert.onClose.description: Called when the close button is pressed. The close button is only drawn when this is set.

components.title: Toast
components.description: A temporary notification that appears in the corner of the screen, with success/error/warning/info types.

props.name: position
props.description: Corner the stack lives in.

props.name: limit
props.description: The maximum number of toasts that can be displayed at once. When the limit is exceeded, the oldest toasts are marked as `limited` (via the `data-limited` attribute) rather than removed, so they can be hidden or animated out.

props.name: timeout
props.description: The default amount of time (in ms) before a toast is auto dismissed. A value of `0` will prevent the toast from being dismissed automatically.

props.name: toastManager
props.description: A global manager for toasts to use outside of a React component.

props.name: className
props.description: CSS class applied to the element, or a function that returns a class based on the component's state.

props.name: render
props.description: Allows you to replace the component's HTML element with a different tag, or compose it with another component. Accepts a `ReactElement` or a function that returns the element to render.

props.name: style
props.description: Style applied to the element, or a function that returns a style object based on the component's state.

parts.name: Toaster
parts.description: The one-line setup. It wraps your app in a provider, renders the viewport and draws every toast, and you pick the corner: top right or bottom right.

parts.name: ToastProvider
parts.description: The provider on its own, with a default timeout of 5000 ms and a stack limit of 3 toasts. Toaster already includes it.

parts.name: ToastViewport
parts.description: The fixed region in the corner, a live region labelled Notifications that holds the stack. Toaster already renders it.

parts.name: Toast
parts.description: One notification, a card with a border and a shadow. Older toasts sit smaller and fainter behind the newest, and hovering or focusing the stack spreads them into a list.

parts.name: Type dot
parts.description: A small dot showing the type: green for success, red for error, yellow for warning and indigo for info.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The bold first line that names the outcome, such as Settings saved.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: One line of detail under the title. It only appears when the toast has a description.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: A text button in the link colour, such as Undo. It only appears when the toast has action props with a label and a click handler.

parts.name: Close button
parts.description: A button named Close that closes the toast at once.

items.text: Write the title as the outcome in a few words, such as Settings saved. Use the description only for detail people need, like what to do next.
Offer Undo for actions people can take back, such as a delete, instead of asking them to confirm first.
Use the promise helper for work that takes a while, so one toast goes from loading to success or error.
Add the Toaster once, high in the app, and call the useToast hook only below it.
Don't use a toast for a problem people have to fix. It goes away, so keep an Alert on the page until the cause is gone.
Don't put information in a toast that appears nowhere else. It can be missed or closed, so the result must also show on the page.
Don't fire several toasts for one action. Merge them into one message, since the stack shows three at a time.
Don't make many toasts stay forever with a timeout of 0. Keep that for a warning people must act on.

useFor: A short confirmation after an action: saved, copied, sent, or deleted with an Undo
The progress of work that runs in the background, from its start to its result
A message that needs no answer and does no harm if it goes unnoticed

useInstead.name: Alert
useInstead.text: a message that belongs to the page and stays until the cause is fixed

useInstead.name: Alert Dialog
useInstead.text: a decision people must make before they can go on

keyboard.intro: A toast never takes focus from what people are doing. It joins the tab order only when people ask for it with F6.

rows.action: Moves focus to the toasts, the region named Notifications.
Goes through each toast, then its action and its close button.
Presses the focused action or close button.
Closes the focused toast.

behavior.intro: How toasts are added, how long they stay, how they stack and what they announce.

items.title: Adding a toast
items.text: The useToast hook returns the manager of the nearest Toaster, with add, close, update, promise and the list of toasts. Adding takes a title, description, type, action, timeout and priority.

items.title: Timing
items.text: A toast closes after 5 seconds, and you can set a timeout or 0 to keep it until closed. The timer pauses while the pointer is over the stack, focus is inside it or the window is in the background.

items.title: Stack
items.text: The newest toast is in front, and older ones sit lower, smaller and fainter behind it. Hovering or focusing the stack spreads them into a list, and it shows three at a time.

items.title: Promise
items.text: The promise helper adds a loading toast that doesn't close by itself, then turns it into the success or error toast when the promise settles. A loading toast has no coloured dot.

items.title: Announcing
items.text: The viewport is a polite live region, so a screen reader reads each new toast without interrupting. Give an urgent toast high priority and it is announced as an alert.

items.title: Position and size
items.text: The stack sits 16 px from the top or bottom right corner. A toast is up to 420 px wide, narrower on a small screen, and can be swiped away on touch.

items.title: Previews in these docs
items.text: A toast is fixed to the screen corner. Each preview here is a framed box standing in for the screen, so toasts come in at its corner and stay inside, and it starts with one toast that stays open.

items.title: Opening and closing
items.text: A toast slides in from the right while fading in, and leaves the same way, at slow speed. The stack moves into place on the same timing.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion toasts don't slide or scale. They only fade in and out.

minimalUsage.intro: Then use it. Wrap your app in the Toaster once, and call the hook anywhere below it:
minimalUsage.expected: A Save button. Pressing it slides a toast into the top right corner of the screen, and it goes away after 5 seconds.

Toaster.position.description: The corner the stack lives in: `top-right` or `bottom-right`. `top-right` by default.

ToastProvider.timeout.description: How long a toast stays before it closes, in milliseconds. 5000 by default; `0` keeps toasts until they are closed. A single toast can set its own `timeout`.

ToastProvider.limit.description: The most toasts that are shown at once. Older ones wait behind the others and are marked `data-limited`. 3 by default.

ToastProvider.toastManager.description: A toast manager created outside React, so toasts can be added from code that is not a component, such as a fetch wrapper.

ToastViewport.position.description: The corner the viewport is fixed to: `top-right` or `bottom-right`. `top-right` by default.

components.title: Pull to Refresh
components.description: Drag down from the top of any content past a threshold to trigger an async refresh, with a rotating spinner and a rubber-band release.
components.props: function PullToRefresh({ onRefresh, onError, threshold, maxPull, children, className, }: PullToRefreshProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: onError
props.description: Called when `onRefresh` throws or its promise rejects. The indicator resets either way and the rejection is not left unhandled; without `onError` the failure is swallowed here, so show it in your own UI.

parts.name: PullToRefresh
parts.description: A clipping box around your content. Give it a height and a background, since the indicator sits behind the content and shows as it moves down.

parts.name: Indicator
parts.description: The spinner icon at the top of the box. It fades in and turns with the pull, then spins until the refresh settles.

parts.name: Content
parts.description: The wrapper around your content that moves down with the pull. It takes the pointer events, lets the browser keep scrolling the content up, and shows a grab cursor, so text inside cannot be selected.

items.text: Return the promise from the refresh handler. The spinner and the lock stay until it settles, so a slow request never looks finished.
Pass an error handler and show the failure in text, such as Couldn't refresh. The component resets after a failure but shows nothing itself, and without a handler the failure is swallowed silently.
Put a visible Refresh button beside the list that calls the same function. The gesture is pointer-based, with no keyboard route and no announcement.
Announce the result in a status line, such as Updated just now. The component says nothing to assistive technology.
Give the box a height, a background and content that fills it. The box clips what moves out of it, and its background shows behind the content during the pull.
Keep the threshold at or below the maximum pull (defaults 70 and 110). The pull moves at half the finger speed, so people drag about twice the threshold.
Don't make the gesture the only way to refresh. Many people use a keyboard, a switch or a screen reader, and on a desktop mouse the drag is easy to miss.
Don't use it for data that updates by itself. Show the new state instead and skip the gesture.
Don't put text people should select inside the content. A drag must not select text, so the content blocks selection and nothing there can be copied.
Don't expect a tap to work right after a pull. The click that ends a drag is swallowed on purpose, so the item under the finger is not opened.

useFor: A touch-first list or feed that people reload by hand, such as an inbox or a notification list
Content that a server owns and that goes stale, such as figures or a status board
A mobile layout where a Refresh button would take room from the list

useInstead.name: Button
useInstead.text: a refresh that must work with a keyboard or a screen reader, on its own or beside the list

useInstead.name: Spinner
useInstead.text: a load with no gesture, such as a page or a panel that is loading

useInstead.name: Pagination
useInstead.text: a long list that people move through page by page

keyboard.intro: PullToRefresh is a pointer gesture. It adds no tab stop, key handling or announcement, so the keyboard route is a button that you provide.
keyboard.note: The content area is not focusable and does not react to Arrow keys, Page Up or Page Down. Scrolling a list inside it works as usual.

rows.action: Moves focus through the controls inside the content and the Refresh button beside it. The wrapper itself is skipped.
On your Refresh button: runs the same function as `onRefresh`. Show its pending state with `pending` on Button.

behavior.intro: What the gesture does with scrolling, taps, the request and motion.

items.title: When a pull starts
items.text: A press becomes a pull only after it moves 8 px, mostly downward, with everything above scrolled to the top. Until then a tap stays a tap, and sideways or upward movement goes back to the browser.

items.title: Mouse and touch
items.text: With a finger the page must be at its top too, because a finger scrolls the page. A mouse drag never scrolls, and only the primary pointer starts a pull, so a second finger is ignored.

items.title: Scrolling content
items.text: Inside content that is scrolled down, the downward gesture scrolls it back up first. At the top the browser leaves the downward pull to the component but keeps horizontal scrolling and pinch zoom.

items.title: Resistance
items.text: The content follows the pointer at half speed and stops at the maximum pull. The indicator fades in and turns with the progress, up to the threshold.

items.title: Release
items.text: If the content has moved at least the threshold, it settles there, the spinner turns and the refresh runs. Below it, the content springs back; presses are ignored during a refresh.

items.title: Failure
items.text: When the refresh fails, the spinner stops, the content springs back and the error handler is called, so the pull never stays locked. Without one the failure is swallowed, so tell people yourself.

items.title: Cancel
items.text: If the browser takes the gesture, for example for a system swipe, the pointer is released and the content springs back without refreshing.

items.title: The click after a pull
items.text: The release that ends a pull is not a click: it is swallowed once, so the row under the finger does not open. The next press clears it.

items.title: Motion
items.text: While the pointer is down the content moves with it and has no transition. After release it settles with a slow ease, and the spinner turns while the refresh runs.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the content jumps to the threshold on release and back when the refresh ends, and the spinner stays a static icon. Pair it with a text status, since a static icon is not a signal.

minimalUsage.expected: You should see the text Pull down to refresh. Drag it down past about 140 px and release: a spinner turns for a second and the text reads Updated just now.

PullToRefresh.onRefresh.description: Called once when the content is released past `threshold`. Return a promise: the spinner turns and the pull stays locked until it settles, also when it rejects or throws, which is reported to `onError`.

PullToRefresh.onError.description: Called with the error when `onRefresh` throws or its promise rejects. The indicator has already reset. Optional: without it the failure is swallowed, so show it in your own UI.

PullToRefresh.threshold.description: How far the content must have moved, in px, before a release refreshes. It is also the height of the indicator area and where the content rests while refreshing. Defaults to 70.

PullToRefresh.maxPull.description: The most the content can move, in px. The pull moves at half the pointer speed, so this takes about twice as much dragging. Keep it at or above `threshold`. Defaults to 110.

PullToRefresh.children.description: The content that is pulled down. Taps reach it normally; a drag that has begun does not click anything.

PullToRefresh.className.description: Extra classes for the outer box (`relative overflow-hidden`), for example a height and a background such as `h-64 bg-bg-page`.

components.title: Rating
components.description: An interactive star rating input.

props.name: aria-label
props.description: Names the group ("Rating" by default); read-only, it replaces "Rated 3.5 out of 5".

props.name: aria-labelledby
props.description: Id of a visible label that names the group, instead of `aria-label`.

props.name: size
props.description: `sm`: the compact 12 px display of a read-only star or heart row. Ignored while the rating is interactive.

parts.name: Rating
parts.description: The group of options. Interactive it is a radio group with one Tab stop, and read-only it is a single image that reads Rated 3.5 out of 5, named by an aria-label.

parts.name: Option
parts.description: One radio of the group: a star or heart (24 px), a face (48 px) or a scale number (40 px high). Hover previews the fill of stars and hearts, and a click or arrow key chooses.

parts.name: Filled icon
parts.description: A star in the yellow brand tone or a heart in the pink one, filled up to the value.

parts.name: Empty icon
parts.description: The outline in the control border colour for the options beyond the value.

parts.name: Value label
parts.description: The number beside the row, on the left or right. The tooltip option shows it in a dark bubble with an arrow above the chosen option instead.

parts.name: RatingCell
parts.description: A read-only star row with the value on the right, made for table cells.

items.text: Pick the type for the question: stars for an opinion, hearts for favorites, emojis for a mood, and scale for a 0 to 10 survey answer such as Net Promoter Score.
Give every interactive Rating a visible question and tie it with aria-labelledby, or set an aria-label. The default name is only Rating.
Set read-only when you display an average. A fractional value such as 3.5 fills the nearest icon and keeps the exact number in the accessible name.
Show the label on the right when the number matters. Without it, a score of 4.5 is only a row of icons.
Show a comment field after a low score, so people can say what went wrong. Send the score only when they confirm it.
Don't use the tooltip label against the top edge of a container. The bubble floats about 32 px above the row and takes no space in the layout, so leave room for it.
Don't expect hover to choose. It only previews the fill of stars and hearts; a click or arrow key chooses, and arrows move and choose in one step.
Don't use the emojis type for a required answer. Clicking the chosen face again clears it and sends 0.

useFor: Asking for an opinion about an article, a template or a purchase, with stars or hearts
A survey answer from 0 to 10, such as how likely someone is to recommend you
Showing an average score beside a product or a review, as a read-only row

useInstead.name: Slider
useInstead.text: picking a value on a continuous range, such as a price or a volume

useInstead.name: Emoji Reaction Button
useInstead.text: a quick reaction to a piece of content, with a count

useInstead.name: Progress
useInstead.text: a share or a completion rather than an opinion

keyboard.intro: An interactive Rating is a radio group of native buttons: one Tab stop, and Arrow keys do the moving. A read-only Rating takes no focus.

rows.action: Moves focus into the group, to the chosen option or to the first one, and out of it. The other options are skipped.
Moves to the next option and chooses it. The arrows stop at the last option and do not wrap. In right-to-left layouts ArrowLeft goes forward.
Moves to the previous option and chooses it. The arrows stop at the first option.
Chooses the first or the last option.
Chooses the focused option. On the faces, pressing it again on the chosen face clears the answer.

behavior.intro: What the rating does with its value, hover, labels and motion.

items.title: Controlled
items.text: Rating keeps no state. The value comes from you, and every choice calls the change handler with the new number, so nothing changes until you set the value.

items.title: Values
items.text: Stars, hearts and faces start at 1 and use 0 for nothing chosen. The scale starts at 0, which is an answer, so pass a value outside its range while nothing is chosen yet.

items.title: Fractions
items.text: A fractional value fills the nearest whole icon (3.2 fills three, 4.5 fills five), and the label keeps the number rounded to one decimal. A read-only row names the exact value.

items.title: Hover
items.text: Hovering a star or a heart previews the fill up to it and returns to the value when the pointer leaves. Faces and numbers only change their background.

items.title: Faces
items.text: Five faces, one answer. Choosing the chosen face again clears the value to 0.

items.title: Scale
items.text: Eleven options from 0 to 10 in a 480 px row that never grows past its container. Below 352 px they wrap into two rows, so use a left or right label instead of the tooltip on a narrow screen.

items.title: Labels
items.text: Left and right put the number beside the row. The tooltip shows it in a dark bubble with an arrow above the chosen option, and the bubble is hidden from assistive technology.

items.title: Read-only
items.text: Read-only renders one image, named Rated 3.5 out of 5 or by your aria-label. The options are plain spans without hover, focus or a Tab stop.

items.title: Direction
items.text: In right-to-left layouts ArrowLeft goes forward and ArrowRight goes back. The order of the icons follows the document direction.

items.title: Motion
items.text: Stars and hearts change their fill at once. Faces and numbers fade their background quickly, and nothing moves or scales.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: There is no movement to remove, so reduced motion changes nothing. The background changes are short fades and stay.

minimalUsage.expected: You should see five empty stars. Click the fourth, or focus the row and press ArrowRight four times, and four stars fill with the yellow brand tone.

Rating.type.description: What the options look like: `stars` (default), `hearts`, `emojis` for five faces or `scale` for a 0 to 10 row.

Rating.value.description: The current value, a controlled number. Stars, hearts and faces count from 1 and use 0 for nothing; the scale counts from 0. A fraction fills the nearest icon.

Rating.onValueChange.description: Called with the number the person chose, by click or arrow key. Choosing the chosen face again sends 0. Without it the rating cannot change.

Rating.label.description: Where the value is shown: `none` (default), `left` or `right` of the row, or `tooltip` in a bubble above the chosen option.

Rating.max.description: The number of stars or hearts, 5 by default. For the scale it is the number of options, 11 by default, so the highest answer is `max - 1`. It has no effect on the faces.

Rating.readOnly.description: Shows the score as one image without focus or hover. Use it for an average.

Rating.className.description: Extra classes for the root, for example `justify-center` or a width for the scale.

RatingCell.value.description: The score to show, as a number up to `max`. A fraction fills the nearest star and the number is written on the right.

RatingCell.max.description: The number of stars in the row, 5 by default.

Rating.size.description: `md` (default) is the 24 px target of an input. `sm` is the compact display of a read-only star or heart row: 12 px icons with a filled grey for the empty ones, for a product card or a review line. It is ignored while the rating is interactive and for faces and the scale. It replaces Stars.

components.title: Trend Chip
components.description: A small pill showing a change, up or down, in seven icon styles.

props.name: direction
props.description: Figma Trend Chip · Trend; `flat` is the old name for `neutral`.

props.name: icon
props.description: Figma Trend Chip · Icon; the same glyph turns for `down`. Default `arrow-diagonal`: up-right for a rise, down-right for a fall.

props.name: sentiment
props.description: Figma Trend Chip · Sentiment: whether the change is good or bad. `auto` colours by direction (up green, down red); use `positive` for a fall that is good (churn, cost) or `negative` for a rise that is bad. The arrow always follows `directi…

parts.name: TrendChip
parts.description: An inline span with a glyph and a label. It isn't interactive and holds no state, so you pass the finished label, the direction and, when colour shouldn't follow direction, the sentiment.

parts.name: Pill
parts.description: The rounded surface, 20 px high. Its colour comes from the sentiment: green tint for positive, red for negative, grey for neutral.

parts.name: Glyph
parts.description: One of seven icons. The same glyph turns for down and a neutral chip always shows a minus, and the glyph follows the text colour and is hidden from screen readers.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The value text in 12 px semibold. It is the only part a screen reader reads, so it carries the sign and the unit.

parts.name: TrendCaret
parts.description: The filled triangle behind the triangle icon, also used by the change label of Number Value. It is exported for your own layouts and is decorative.

items.text: Write the sign and unit into the value: +12.4%, -3 pts, +$1,204. The glyph is hidden from screen readers, so the label is all they get.
Keep direction and meaning apart. Direction sets which way the glyph points and sentiment sets the colour: falling churn is down and positive, a rising ticket count is up and negative.
Choose one icon style per screen and keep it. The padding follows the glyph, so mixed styles in a column don't line up.
Name what the change is measured against, in the chip (+4.2% vs last month) or in the text beside it. A change without a reference says little.
Don't leave sentiment on auto for a metric where a fall is good. Auto colours by direction, so a falling error rate would show red.
Don't rely on colour alone. Green and red don't reach everyone, so the sign in the label and the glyph direction say the same thing.
Don't use it for a status or a count. A chip shows a change, so for a state such as Paid or Failed use Badge.
Don't use flat as a direction in new code. It is the old name for neutral.

useFor: The change of a figure in a table cell, a card header or a list row
A percentage, a number of points or an amount that went up or down since a reference
A compact pill where the figure itself sits in your own markup

useInstead.name: Number Value
useInstead.text: a headline figure with its change as one unit

useInstead.name: Badge
useInstead.text: a status or a count, such as Paid or 3 new

useInstead.name: Meter
useInstead.text: a figure measured against a limit, such as storage used

behavior.intro: What the chip renders and how it reads.

items.title: Static
items.text: TrendChip isn't interactive, with no focus, hover state or handlers. Wrap it in your own link or button where the change should open something.

items.title: Colour follows the sentiment
items.text: By default a rise is green and a fall is red. Positive makes the chip green and negative red whatever the direction, neutral makes it grey, and the glyph always follows the direction, not the colour.

items.title: Neutral
items.text: A neutral direction shows a minus and, on auto, a grey chip, and the icon choice has no effect on it. Flat is the old name for neutral.

items.title: Glyphs
items.text: The icon picks one of seven glyphs. For down, the same glyph turns: the trend line mirrors, arrows point down, the triangle rotates 180 degrees and the circled diagonal a quarter turn.

items.title: Size and spacing
items.text: The pill is 20 px high with 8 px padding on the glyph side. Glyph to label is 4 px for the 12 px glyph, 6 px for 14 px circles and 8 px for 16 px arrows and the triangle.

items.title: Reading
items.text: A screen reader reads the label as plain text, for example +12.4%. The glyph is hidden and colour isn't announced, so the sign has to be in the string.

items.title: Numbers
items.text: The label isn't formatted for you. Use English format with a comma, 1,284, and add tabular figures in a column of changing values so the chips keep their width.

items.title: Motion
items.text: None. The chip appears as it is and doesn't animate when its value, direction or colour changes.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: There is no motion, so reduced motion changes nothing.

minimalUsage.expected: A small green pill with a rising trend line and +12.4%.

TrendChip.value.description: The label of the chip, as a finished string with its sign and unit, for example `+12.4%` or `-1.8 pts`. It is not formatted for you.

TrendChip.direction.description: Which way the glyph points. `neutral` shows a minus and ignores `icon`; `flat` is the old name for `neutral`. Defaults to `up`.

TrendChip.icon.description: The glyph: `trending`, `arrow`, `arrow-diagonal`, `triangle`, `circle-trending`, `circle-diagonal` or `circle-arrow`. The same glyph turns for `down`. Defaults to `arrow-diagonal`.

TrendChip.sentiment.description: Whether the change is good or bad, which sets the colour. `auto` colours by direction: up green, down red, neutral grey. Use `positive` for a fall that is good and `negative` for a rise that is bad. It does not change the glyph. Defaults to `auto`.

TrendChip.className.description: Extra classes for the pill, for example `tabular-nums` in a column of figures or a different gap.

TrendCaret.down.description: Turns the triangle 180 degrees so it points down. Defaults to false.

TrendCaret.large.description: Draws the 14 px caret of Number Value instead of the 16 px caret of the chip. Defaults to false.

TrendCaret.className.description: Extra classes for the SVG, for example a colour from the text roles.

components.title: Pressable Feedback
components.description: Wraps any content with a scale-down press animation.

props.name: asChild
props.description: Apply the press effect to the child element instead of wrapping it.

parts.name: PressableFeedback
parts.description: Scales its content to 95 % at 90 % opacity while pressed. Alone it renders a button, with asChild it lends the effect to its single child, and it adds a focus ring only.

parts.name: Content
parts.description: What you pass as children: a label, an icon with a label, a card body. It scales together with the button.

items.text: Use it to give press feedback to something that is not a button yet, such as a tile, card or row. Buttons and icon buttons already react to a press.
Pass asChild when the child is already a button or a link. Without it you nest a button inside a button, which is invalid HTML.
Handle the action with the press handler. With asChild the child's own click handler runs first, then the press handler.
Give the pressable its own look: a border, a fill and a hover tone. The component only adds the scale, the opacity and the focus ring.
Don't put links or other buttons inside it without asChild. They would sit inside a button, and nested interactive elements break.
Don't use it for a disabled state or a name that is not in the content. Its own button takes neither; use asChild and put them on the child.
Don't use it on a large surface, such as a whole panel. A 5 % scale of a wide element moves its edges visibly.

useFor: Tiles, cards and rows that people press, such as quick actions or a template picker
A link or a button of your own that should react to a press the way the library buttons do
Touch layouts, where a press needs to be seen at once under the finger

useInstead.name: Button
useInstead.text: a normal action; it already reacts to a press

useInstead.name: Icon Button
useInstead.text: an action that is only an icon

useInstead.name: Card
useInstead.text: a surface that holds content, with an interactive mode for whole-card links

keyboard.intro: Without asChild it is a native button, so the browser provides focus and activation. With asChild the keys are those of the child.

rows.action: Moves focus to the pressable and away from it. The focus ring shows while it is focused.
Activates a button or a link and calls `onPress`. Enter does not hold the pressed look; only the click runs.
Holds the pressed look while the key is down on a button, and activates it on release.

behavior.intro: What the pressable does while it is held, with a mouse, a finger or a key, and how it relates to its child.

items.title: Pressed
items.text: Pressing the mouse button sets the pressed look, 95 % scale at 90 % opacity, and releasing or leaving the element returns it. A finger and the Space key get the same look.

items.title: Own button
items.text: Alone it renders a button around its children and calls the press handler on click. It takes no other attributes, so it cannot be disabled or labelled: its content names it.

items.title: asChild
items.text: With asChild and one element as child, the effect goes onto that child: class names merge and its own handlers still run. A non-element child falls back to the own button.

items.title: Hover
items.text: There is no hover look of its own. Add one to the content.

items.title: Focus
items.text: The focus ring is the standard one: an indigo border with a 2 px ring, shown for keyboard focus.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The scale animates with the fast duration and the move easing, so a press answers at once and springs back softly.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the transition is removed. The scale and opacity still apply instantly, so a press is seen without anything moving.

minimalUsage.expected: You should see a bordered tile that says New invoice. Hold the mouse button on it and it shrinks a little; release and it springs back and logs opened.

PressableFeedback.children.description: The content to scale. With `asChild` it must be a single element, which receives the effect.

PressableFeedback.onPress.description: Called when the pressable is activated, from the click. With `asChild` it runs after the child's own `onClick`.

PressableFeedback.className.description: Extra classes for the button, or merged into the child with `asChild`. This is where the look goes: border, fill, padding and hover.

components.title: Emoji Reaction Button
components.description: A toggleable emoji reaction with a count, like a Slack reaction.
components.props: function EmojiReactionButton({ emoji, icon, label, count, active, onToggle, onClick, className, ...props }: EmojiReactionButtonProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: emoji
props.description: The reaction as an emoji. Leave it out and pass `icon` where the product shows no emoji.

props.name: icon
props.description: The reaction as an icon (14 px, e.g. a thumbs up), in place of `emoji`.

props.name: label
props.description: What the reaction means ("Agree", "Thanks"): the accessible name is "<label>: <count>". Needed with an `icon`, which has no text of its own; `aria-label` replaces it entirely.

parts.name: EmojiReactionButton
parts.description: A native button that shows an emoji and a count and reports whether it is pressed. It is controlled: you hold the active state and count and change them in the toggle handler.

parts.name: Pill
parts.description: The 26 px high capsule with a 1 px border and a small gap between emoji and count. Off, it has a neutral border and secondary text; on, an indigo tint with indigo border and text.

parts.name: Emoji
parts.description: The emoji character, at the text size of the pill. It is part of the button's accessible name, so a screen reader reads the emoji and then the count.

parts.name: Count
parts.description: The number of people who reacted, shown as a plain number after the emoji. It does not change by itself when pressed, so update it in the toggle handler.

items.text: Keep the active state and the count together and change them in the toggle handler: turning on adds one, turning off takes one away.
Show only the reactions that exist, and open an Emoji Picker from a small icon button for the rest. A reaction that drops to zero should disappear.
Put the buttons in a wrapping row with a gap, so they wrap on a narrow screen instead of overflowing.
Don't use it as a general toggle. It is for a reaction with a count; for an on or off option in a toolbar use Toggle.
Don't show a count of zero. A reaction nobody has chosen is not shown, and the Emoji Picker adds it again.
Don't use an emoji as the only information. Where the meaning matters, say it in text near the buttons.
Where the product shows no emoji, pass an icon and a label; the label names the button ("Agree: 3").

useFor: Reactions under a message, a comment, a post or a changelog entry
Quick feedback with a visible tally, such as helpful or not helpful
A small set of choices where people see how many others chose the same

useInstead.name: Toggle
useInstead.text: an on or off option for the person alone, such as bold or mute

useInstead.name: Rating
useInstead.text: a score from one to five

useInstead.name: Badge
useInstead.text: a read-only label or count that cannot be pressed

keyboard.intro: The button is a native button, so the browser provides focus and activation.

rows.action: Moves focus to the next or previous reaction. Each one is a tab stop.
Switches the reaction on or off by calling `onToggle`. The screen reader announces the new pressed state.

behavior.intro: What the button does with state, names and motion.

items.title: Controlled
items.text: The button keeps no state. The active state and count come from you, and every press calls the toggle handler without arguments, so nothing changes until you update them.

items.title: Pressed state
items.text: The pressed state follows the active one, so assistive technology announces pressed or not pressed. A reaction is a toggle, not a link or a menu.

items.title: Name
items.text: The accessible name is the emoji followed by the count, for example fire 12. It cannot be overridden, so say what the reaction means in text near the row.

items.title: States
items.text: Off has a neutral border, secondary text and hover and pressed fills; on has an indigo tint, border and text. Focus shows the indigo border and a 2 px ring.

items.title: Size
items.text: The pill is 26 px high with 8 px of side padding and 12 px text. It does not grow with the count, it only gets one digit wider at a time.

items.title: Numbers
items.text: The count is a plain number, so 1284 reads 1284. For large counts keep the figure short, or show a tally of your own beside the buttons.

items.title: Motion
items.text: Border, fill and text colour fade on the fast duration when the state changes. Nothing moves or scales.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: There is no movement to remove, so reduced motion changes nothing. The colour change is a short fade and stays.

minimalUsage.expected: You see a pill with a fire emoji and a count of 11. Press it and it turns indigo with the count at 12; press again to go back.

EmojiReactionButton.emoji.description: The emoji to show, as a character. It is the first part of the button's accessible name.

EmojiReactionButton.count.description: The number of people who reacted. It is shown as a plain number and does not change on its own: update it together with `active`.

EmojiReactionButton.active.description: Whether the reaction is switched on. It sets `aria-pressed` and the indigo tint. Off by default.

EmojiReactionButton.onToggle.description: Called without arguments when the button is pressed. Flip `active` and change the count here.

EmojiReactionButton.className.description: Extra classes for the button, for example a margin in a row.

components.title: Emoji Picker
components.description: A grid of selectable emoji, typically shown inside a Popover.

parts.name: EmojiPicker
parts.description: A panel with a grid of emoji buttons, in a group named Emoji. It keeps no state: it hands the pressed emoji to your handler and you decide what happens next.

parts.name: Panel
parts.description: The card around the grid: a border, the popover surface, a shadow and 16 px corners. Six columns with 4 px between them and 8 px of padding make a row 230 px wide.

parts.name: Emoji button
parts.description: A 32 px button with 8 px corners, named by its emoji. Hover fills it with the page tone, pressed with the subtle tone, and keyboard focus shows the indigo border and 2 px ring.

items.text: Put the picker inside a Popover opened by an icon button and close it on pick. The picker draws its own card, so strip the border, background, padding and shadow from the popover content.
Pass a short list of emoji in a fixed order. The grid has six columns, so 6, 12 or 18 emoji fill every row.
Give the trigger an accessible name such as Add a reaction. The picker names its own buttons by their emoji, but the button that opens it needs words.
Don't use it as an emoji keyboard. It shows only the emoji you pass: no search, categories, skin tones or recently used.
Don't use an emoji as the only information in a control. The buttons are named by the emoji alone, so keep visible text where the meaning matters.
Don't expect it to close anything. The picker does not know about the Popover it sits in, so a pick leaves it open until you close it.

useFor: Reactions under a message, a comment or a post, where one tap adds an emoji
A short, curated set of emoji to label or mood-tag something
Inserting an emoji into a comment box or a status line

useInstead.name: Rating
useInstead.text: a score from one to five rather than a free choice of emoji

useInstead.name: Combobox
useInstead.text: a long list that people search by typing

useInstead.name: Dropdown Menu
useInstead.text: a list of actions with text labels

keyboard.intro: Every emoji is a native button, so the browser provides focus and activation. The picker adds no arrow key navigation: each button is one tab stop.

rows.action: Moves focus to the next or previous emoji, left to right and top to bottom.
Picks the focused emoji and calls `onSelect` with it.
In a Popover: closes it and returns focus to the trigger. The picker itself does nothing on Escape.

behavior.intro: What the picker does with state, layout, names and motion.

items.title: No state
items.text: The picker does not remember a pick, show a selected emoji or close anything. Every press hands you the emoji, and what follows is yours: store it, insert it, close the Popover.

items.title: Layout
items.text: Six columns with 4 px between them, 32 px buttons and 8 px of padding. Fewer than six emoji leave the panel 230 px wide, more than six wrap onto new rows, and there is no maximum height or scrolling.

items.title: Names
items.text: The group is named Emoji and each button is named by its emoji, so a screen reader reads the standard name, such as fire. A custom picture is not announced like that, so use real emoji characters.

items.title: The default set
items.text: By default the picker shows twelve: grinning face, tears of joy, heart eyes, thumbs up, folded hands, fire, party popper, red heart, crying face, open mouth, clapping hands and rocket.

items.title: Surface
items.text: The panel uses the popover surface with a border and a large shadow, because it normally floats. Inside a card you can lay it flat by removing the shadow.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The picker has no motion of its own: hover and pressed fills change at once. A Popover around it fades and scales in, and out a step faster.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the Popover keeps its fade and drops the scale. The picker has nothing to remove.

minimalUsage.expected: You see a card with twelve emoji in two rows of six. Press one and its emoji appears after the word Picked.

EmojiPicker.emojis.description: The emoji to show, one string each, in order. Defaults to twelve common reactions. The grid has six columns, so a multiple of six fills every row. Each emoji must be unique, because it is the key.

EmojiPicker.onSelect.description: Called with the emoji that was pressed. The picker keeps no selection, so store the emoji, insert it or close the Popover here.

EmojiPicker.className.description: Extra classes for the panel, for example `shadow-none` inside a card or a different `grid-cols-*`.

components.title: Checklist Task
components.description: One step of an onboarding checklist that can be ticked off, with the next step to do highlighted.

props.name: action
props.description: A button shown on the current step, e.g. "Start".

props.name: current
props.description: The step to do next — tinted, with room for `meta` and an `action`.

props.name: onClick
props.description: Toggle the step.

parts.name: ChecklistTask
parts.description: The row: 12 px side padding, 8 px radius and 12 px between its parts. A done or open step is one checkbox button, while the current step is a tinted block with two buttons.

parts.name: Circle
parts.description: A 22 px circle: empty with a 1.5 px rim while open, indigo rim on the current step, solid green with a tick when done. On the current step it is its own checkbox button named Mark as done.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The label in 14 px medium text. It is quiet (tertiary) when the step is done and takes the tint of the row on the current step.

parts.name: Meta
parts.description: The meta line under the label, in 12 px text, for example the time a step takes. It is shown in every state.

parts.name: Action
parts.description: The action, usually a Start button, at the right of the current step. The other states do not render it.

parts.name: Chevron
parts.description: A 16 px chevron at the right of an open step that is not current. A done step and the current step have none.

items.text: Use Checklist Task for the steps of an onboarding or setup checklist. For a plain list of options without a next step, use Checkbox Field.
Mark exactly one step current and give it an action such as Start. Only the current step shows the action, and its circle becomes a checkbox button of its own.
Handle the click as a toggle. It fires for open and done steps alike, so a step can be ticked and unticked again.
Work out the current step from the list, as the first step that is not done, so it moves on by itself when a step is ticked.
Put the steps in a list. Inside a panel with 8 px of padding and a 16 px radius, the 8 px row is concentric to the panel.
After a tick, move focus back to the checkbox of the step that was pressed. The current step is rebuilt as another element, so a step that becomes or stops being current loses focus.
Don't pass an action to steps that are not current. It is not rendered there.
Don't use a step for something that cannot be ticked yet. There is no disabled state, so leave the step out until it can be done.

useFor: The steps of an onboarding, setup or getting-started checklist
A list where one step is next and has its own button
A short list of tasks that people tick and untick

useInstead.name: Checkbox
useInstead.text: options in a form, with a label and a hint

useInstead.name: Progress
useInstead.text: how far along something is, without naming the steps

useInstead.name: List Item
useInstead.text: a row that opens something, with a leading checkbox among other slots

keyboard.intro: An open or done step is one tab stop, and the current step has two: its circle, then its action. Both are native buttons, so Enter and Space work on them.
keyboard.note: Arrow keys do not move between steps. Build the steps as a list and let Tab walk through them.

rows.action: Moves focus to the next or previous step. On the current step it visits the circle first and the action second.
Toggles the focused step and calls `onClick`. On the current step, the circle toggles it and the action does whatever you gave it.

behavior.intro: What the row does with state, content, the DOM and motion.

items.title: Three states, two kinds of element
items.text: An open or done step is one checkbox button. The current step is a block holding two buttons, the circle (Mark as done) and your action, and done and current can be set together.

items.title: Hover
items.text: Hovering an open or done step fills the row lightly, and the circle of an open step turns indigo. The current step has no hover fill, because its action is the thing to press.

items.title: Focus
items.text: Keyboard focus draws an indigo border with a 2 px ring around the row, or around the circle on the current step. The ring follows the rounded shape.

items.title: Long text
items.text: The label and meta wrap and the row grows. The action keeps its size, so the text gives way, and a word without a break point is not cut.

items.title: Names for assistive technology
items.text: An open or done step is named by its label followed by its meta. The current step's circle is always named Mark as done, so give the Start button its own label.

items.title: Focus after a tick
items.text: A step that becomes or stops being current is rebuilt as another element, and the focused button disappears. Return focus to the checkbox of the step the person pressed.

items.title: Motion and reduced motion
items.text: Colours of the row, circle and label change quickly, and the green tick scales in once with a fade. With reduced motion it only fades in, and the colours still change.

minimalUsage.expected: You see one row with an empty circle, the label with 3 min under it and a chevron. Pressing it turns the circle green, adds a tick and dims the label.

ChecklistTask.children.description: The label of the step. Required.

ChecklistTask.done.description: Draws a green circle with a tick and a quiet label, and sets `aria-checked`. Without it the step is open.

ChecklistTask.current.description: Marks the step to do next: tinted row, circle as its own checkbox button, room for `action`. Use it on one step.

ChecklistTask.meta.description: A line under the label, for example how long the step takes. Shown in every state.

ChecklistTask.action.description: A button at the right of the current step, for example Start. Not rendered on a step that is not current.

ChecklistTask.onClick.description: Toggles the step. On an open or done step it is the row; on the current step it is the circle. Called for ticking and unticking alike.

ChecklistTask.className.description: Added to the row. Use it for the width or for spacing in a list.

components.title: Text Link Row
components.description: A line of text followed by a link, like “Don't have an account? Sign up”, or a back link with an arrow.
components.props: function TextLinkRow({ text, link, href, onLinkClick, variant, className, }: TextLinkRowProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: text
props.description: Leading copy, e.g. "Don't have an account?"

props.name: link
props.description: Link label, e.g. "Sign up". Omitted for Type=back.

props.name: variant
props.description: inline (14px) · small (12px) · stacked (two lines, centered) · icon (help icon + small) · back (arrow, no link)

parts.name: TextLinkRow
parts.description: A paragraph that lays its children out in one flex line, centred, 4 px apart. It is as wide as its container, starts at the left and has no border or background.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: A 16 px help icon in front of the text, only in the icon variant. It sits 8 px from the text.

parts.name: Text
parts.description: The text in a span: 14 px secondary for inline, 12 px tertiary for small and icon, 14 px tertiary for stacked.

parts.name: Link
parts.description: The link, semibold in the link colour, 14 px (12 px in small and icon) and underlined on hover. Without a link no anchor is rendered.

items.text: Use it for the quiet line that points to the other way through an auth screen: sign up instead of sign in, resend, change the address, contact support, go back. The main step stays a Button.
Keep the text to one short sentence and the link to one or two words. The text states the situation and the link names where it leads, such as Don't have an account, then Sign up.
Give the link a real href when it goes somewhere, since the default scrolls to the top. For an action that stays on screen, like Resend, handle the click and change the text so people see it worked.
Centre the row under a centred card with justify-center. By default the row fills its container and starts at the left.
Use the back variant for the way out of a step, last on the screen. It carries only text, so a link passed with it is ignored.
Don't put a long sentence in the text. It wraps in its own column and squeezes the link, so in a narrow container let the link wrap under the text.
Don't use it for the main or a destructive action. A text link is easy to miss and has no pressed or loading state, so use a Button.
Don't leave the href at the default for a link you don't handle. The page jumps to the top and the history gets an entry.

useFor: The line under a sign-in or sign-up form that names the other way in, such as Don't have an account? Sign up
A second line of help next to a field or a button, such as Resend, Change email or Contact support
The way back on a verification, reset or code screen

useInstead.name: Button
useInstead.text: the main step of a screen, such as Sign in or Continue

useInstead.name: Alert
useInstead.text: a hint or a warning without a link (size inline), or a message about the screen that needs attention

keyboard.intro: The row itself handles no keys. The link and the back link are native anchors and work the way the browser makes them work.
keyboard.note: A link follows on Enter only. Space doesn't follow a link, as with any link, and the browser may scroll the page instead.

rows.action: Moves focus to the link, or to the back link, and away from it again. The text is skipped.
Follows the focused link to its `href`. With `onLinkClick` the handler runs first; call `preventDefault` there to stay on the page.
Does nothing on a link. The browser may scroll the page.

behavior.intro: What the row does with its parts and its width, and what it leaves to you.

items.title: Variants
items.text: Inline is the 14 px line, small is 12 px tertiary, stacked puts text over the link, icon is small with a help icon, and back is one link with an arrow (an anchor, not a paragraph).

items.title: Link
items.text: The link goes to the href you pass, or to the top of the page by default. The click handler doesn't prevent the default, so app routes call preventDefault, and in back the whole row is the anchor.

items.title: Hover
items.text: The link is underlined on hover, and the back link turns from secondary to full text colour. Neither change is animated.

items.title: Focus
items.text: The back link takes the library's focus ring. The inline link shows the browser's default outline, which the docs theme draws in indigo, and both are visible.

items.title: Width and alignment
items.text: The row fills its container and starts at the left, and justify-center or justify-end moves it. The back variant is as wide as its content, and with items-center on a flex parent the row shrinks.

items.title: Long text
items.text: The text wraps inside its own box and the link keeps what is left, so a long sentence squeezes the link into a word-by-word column. Letting the row wrap moves the whole link under the text.

items.title: Semantics
items.text: The row reads as text followed by a link, and the icon is hidden from assistive technology. Choose link text that makes sense out of context, and wrap changing text in a status region.

items.title: Where it is used
items.text: Sign-in, sign-up, forgot-password, verification, OTP, onboarding and team-invite blocks use it for the line under the form and for the way back.

items.title: Motion and reduced motion
items.text: None. The underline and the back link colour change at once, and reduced motion changes nothing.

minimalUsage.expected: One line of grey text followed by a semibold indigo link. The link is underlined on hover and goes to /sign-up.

TextLinkRow.text.description: The lead-in text, or the label of the back link. Any node; a string is the usual case. Required.

TextLinkRow.link.description: The label of the link after the text. Any node. Without it no anchor is rendered, and the back variant ignores it.

TextLinkRow.href.description: Where the link, or the back link, goes. Default `#`.

TextLinkRow.onLinkClick.description: Called when the link, or the back link, is clicked. The default action is not prevented.

TextLinkRow.variant.description: `inline` is one 14 px line, `small` one 12 px line, `stacked` two centred lines, `icon` a help icon and a 12 px line, `back` an arrow and one link. Default `inline`.

TextLinkRow.className.description: Extra classes for the root: the paragraph, or the anchor in the back variant. For example `justify-center` or `flex-wrap`.

components.title: Social Sign In Buttons
components.description: Sign-in buttons for Google, Apple, GitHub and Microsoft, side by side or stacked.
components.props: function SocialSignInButtons({ providers, layout, prefix, onSelect, className, }: SocialSignInButtonsProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: layout
props.description: horizontal = one row, vertical = stacked full-width buttons

props.name: prefix
props.description: "Continue with" / "Sign in with" prefix; pass "" for icon + name only.

parts.name: SocialSignInButtons
parts.description: A grid with a 12 px gap: horizontal is one column below 640 px window width and one row of equal columns above, vertical is always one column. It has no border, background or role.

parts.name: Button
parts.description: One plain, rounded large Button per provider, as wide as its column. The label is the prefix plus the provider name on one line, or the name alone when the prefix is empty.

parts.name: Mark
parts.description: The provider's 16 px logo before the label, hidden from screen readers. Google and Microsoft keep their brand colours, Apple and GitHub take the text colour.

items.text: Use it where a person picks an account at Google, Apple, GitHub or Microsoft on a sign-in or sign-up screen. The sign-in itself is yours, the component only reports the choice.
Give each button room for its label: about 200 px with the prefix (two per row from 430 px) or 105 to 120 px without (four from 520 px). Otherwise go vertical.
Put a Divider with Label saying or between the buttons and an email form, and use the same prefix on every button of a screen: Sign up with, Continue with or Sign in with.
Show the wait and the failure next to the buttons. Wrap them in a disabled fieldset while a provider is pending, and write what happened, like Google sign-in was cancelled, not Something went wrong.
Offer only providers that work on the screen, since a button that leads nowhere is worse than a missing one. Keep the order the same on every screen.
Don't put three or four providers with a prefix in one row. The label does not wrap or shorten, it runs out of the button over the next one.
Don't draw your own marks or recolour the buttons. The marks follow each provider's brand guidelines, so use the component as it is.
Don't use the buttons to show which accounts are already connected, because they have no selected, connected or loading state. For connections use a list of rows with a button each.

useFor: A sign-in or sign-up card that offers an account at Google, Apple, GitHub or Microsoft
A social-first screen where the providers come before the email form
A row of providers on an invitation or onboarding page

useInstead.name: Button
useInstead.text: any action that is not the choice of a provider, such as Sign in with email

useInstead.name: Divider with Label
useInstead.text: the or between the providers and an email form

useInstead.name: Text Link Row
useInstead.text: a line that leads to the other screen, such as Sign up

keyboard.intro: The component handles no keys itself. Every provider is a native button and a tab stop, in the order you list them, with no arrow key navigation between them.

rows.action: Moves focus to the next or the previous provider, and out of the group after the last one. A button inside a disabled fieldset is skipped.
Presses the focused button and calls `onSelect` with the provider.
Presses the focused button, on release of the key, like any button.

behavior.intro: What the buttons do with their label and width, and what they leave to you.

items.title: Providers
items.text: The providers list sets the buttons in the order you give it, Google and GitHub by default. Each provider can appear once, and an empty list renders an empty grid.

items.title: Layout and width
items.text: Horizontal stacks below 640 px and sits in one row above, by window width, not container width. In a narrow container on a wide window use vertical or fewer providers.

items.title: Label
items.text: The label is the prefix plus the provider name, like Continue with Google, or the name alone with an empty prefix. It stays on one line and runs out of a too-narrow column.

items.title: Press
items.text: A press reports google, apple, github or microsoft. The component starts no sign-in, keeps no state and shows no pending or selected button, and it never submits a surrounding form.

items.title: States
items.text: The buttons are plain Buttons: hover tints the fill, a press scales down a little, focus shows the ring. For a disabled state wrap them in a disabled fieldset, which dims them to 40 %.

items.title: Semantics
items.text: The grid has no role or name, and each button is named by its label. To name the group wrap the buttons in a labelled group, and put a pending or failed status in an always-mounted status element.

items.title: Where it is used
items.text: The split sign-in, centred sign-in, split sign-up, sign-up with password rules and social-first sign-up blocks use it.

items.title: Motion and reduced motion
items.text: Fill and border change quickly, and a press scales the button to 97 %. With reduced motion the scale is off and only the colour changes.

minimalUsage.expected: You see two white buttons side by side on a wide screen, Continue with Google and Continue with GitHub, each with its logo. Pressing one logs the provider.

SocialSignInButtons.providers.description: The buttons to show, in order: `google`, `apple`, `github` or `microsoft`. Default `google` and `github`.

SocialSignInButtons.layout.description: `horizontal` is one row from 640 px of window width and a column below it, `vertical` is always a column. Default `horizontal`.

SocialSignInButtons.prefix.description: The words before the provider name. An empty string leaves the name alone. Default `Continue with`.

SocialSignInButtons.onSelect.description: Called with the provider when its button is pressed. Nothing else happens: start the sign-in here.

SocialSignInButtons.className.description: Extra classes for the grid, for example `w-56` or `max-w-sm`.

components.title: Password Requirement
components.description: One password rule in a checklist that turns green once the password meets it.

parts.name: PasswordRequirement
parts.description: An li in a 12 px flex row with 8 px between icon and label, carrying a met data attribute when the rule is met. It renders no list, so put it inside a ul or ol.

parts.name: Icon
parts.description: A 16 px Lucide icon: a check in a circle in the success colour when the rule is met, an empty circle when it is not. It is hidden from assistive technology.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The rule text, in the secondary colour when met and the tertiary colour when not. Add a visually hidden word for the state, such as met, so a screen reader reads it.

items.text: Put the requirements in a ul with an aria-label such as Password requirements. The component is an li, and a list tells a screen reader how many rules there are.
Add a hidden word after the label for the state, such as met or not met, in a screen-reader-only span. Without it the state is shown by icon and colour only, which a screen reader does not read.
Run every rule on each change and pass the result as met. Keep the rules in one array, so the list and the check that enables the submit button never disagree.
Say the total in a status line next to the list, such as 3 of 4 requirements met. It changes only when the count does, so a screen reader announces progress without reading the list on every key.
Point the password field at the list with aria-describedby, so the rules are read when the field gets focus.
Don't rely on the green icon alone to show a result, since people who cannot see colour miss it and the unmet circle is not an error. Keep the text and the hidden state word.
Don't show an unmet rule as an error before the person has typed. An empty field with every circle empty is the starting point, not a failure.
Don't use it for a checklist of tasks: it is a rule that a value passes or fails. Use Checklist Task for steps someone completes.

useFor: The rules of a new password on a sign-up or a reset form, checked as the person types
Any short list of conditions that a typed value has to meet, such as a username or a workspace address
A list that must stay visible next to the field, so the person sees what is missing before they submit

useInstead.name: Password Strength
useInstead.text: one overall result of how strong a password is, as a meter and a word

useInstead.name: Alert
useInstead.text: an error after a submit, written as a sentence with what to do

useInstead.name: Checkbox
useInstead.text: a list that people tick themselves

behavior.intro: What the component renders and what it leaves to the page.

items.title: Display only
items.text: PasswordRequirement shows a result; it does not test a password, hold state or fire events. You compute met from the value and pass it, and the row changes on the next render.

items.title: States
items.text: When met is true the icon is a green check in a circle and the label uses the secondary colour. When false the icon is an empty circle and the label is tertiary.

items.title: Semantics
items.text: The row is an li, so the list counts the rules. The icon is hidden and the component adds no state text, so a screen reader reads the label only, unless you add a hidden met or not met.

items.title: Announcing changes
items.text: A row that changes colour is not announced. Put a status line with the count of met rules near the list: it is spoken when the number changes, not on every key press.

items.title: Not focusable
items.text: The row is not interactive: no focus, no hover state, not a tab stop. The field it describes is the control.

items.title: Long labels
items.text: The label wraps and is never cut, and the icon is centred on the whole label, so on two lines it sits between them. Align items to the start in the class to keep it beside the first line.

items.title: Sample values
items.text: Use obviously made-up passwords in examples and tests, such as correct-horse-battery. The demos run on local state and send nothing.

items.title: Dark mode
items.text: It uses the theme tokens for the text and the success colour, so it follows the theme.

items.title: Motion
items.text: None. The icon and the colour change at once when met changes; nothing fades or moves.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: There is no motion, so reduced motion changes nothing.

minimalUsage.expected: You see a grey circle with the text At least 8 characters. Pass a password of eight or more characters and the circle turns into a green check.

PasswordRequirement.met.description: Whether the password meets the rule. Required. `true` shows the green check, the secondary text colour and `data-met`; `false` shows the empty circle and the tertiary colour.

PasswordRequirement.children.description: The label of the rule, as text or any content. Add a visually hidden word for the state after it so a screen reader hears whether the rule is met.

PasswordRequirement.className.description: Extra classes for the row, merged after its own. Use them for `items-start` on a label that wraps or a different text size.

components.title: Password Strength
components.description: A four-step meter with a label that shows how strong a password is.

parts.name: PasswordStrength
parts.description: A column with 6 px between the segments and the label, announced politely. It fills the width of its parent, holds no state and tests nothing: you pass the level.

parts.name: Segments
parts.description: A row of four bars, 4 px high with 4 px between them, sharing the width equally. They carry no text and no role: they are drawn, not read.

parts.name: Segment
parts.description: One bar: the first one to four are filled with the colour of the level and the rest use the border colour. Weak fills 1, fair 2, good 3, strong 4.

parts.name: Label
parts.description: The text under the bars in 12 px type, in the colour of the level: Weak password, Fair password, Good password or Strong password, or your own label. It is always shown.

items.text: Get the level from getPasswordStrength and render the meter only when it returns one (null for an empty password). Keep it mounted while the person types, so level changes are announced.
Leave the label on: it says the level in words, so colour is never the only signal, and a screen reader reads the label, not the bars. Pass your own label for other wording or another language.
Reserve the height of the meter and put a hint in it until the first key, as in the sign-up example, so the form does not jump when the meter appears.
Put the meter in a column as wide as the field above it. It fills the width of its parent.
Don't treat the helper as your password policy: it scores only length and character kinds, so Password1! scores strong. Enforce your real rules on the server and show them with Password Requirement.
Don't show a level for a password that is not typed. An empty field has no strength, and a weak bar for an empty field reads as an error.
Don't use real passwords in examples, tests or screenshots; use obviously made-up strings such as correct-horse. The demos keep them in local state and send nothing.

useFor: Quick feedback under a new-password field on a sign-up, a reset or a settings form
One overall result of how strong a password is, in four steps
A meter with a label that a screen reader can read, next to a field the person is typing in

useInstead.name: Password Requirement
useInstead.text: rule-by-rule feedback that shows what is still missing

useInstead.name: Progress
useInstead.text: the progress of a task or an upload

useInstead.name: Meter
useInstead.text: a value inside a known range, such as disk use

behavior.intro: What the meter renders and how it reads.

items.title: Display only
items.text: PasswordStrength shows a level; it does not score a password, hold state or fire events. You pass the strength, and the segments and label change on the next render.

items.title: Levels
items.text: Strength is weak, fair, good or strong, filling one to four segments and colouring segments and label red, amber, blue and green. Unfilled segments use the border colour.

items.title: Scoring helper
items.text: getPasswordStrength gives one point each for 8 characters, 12 characters, mixed case, a digit and a symbol: 1 is weak, 2 fair, 3 good, 4 or 5 strong. It is a hint, not a security measure.

items.title: Text alternative
items.text: The label under the bars is the text alternative: it says the level in words and is always shown, so the meter never rests on colour alone. The bars have no role, so a screen reader reads the label.

items.title: Announcing changes
items.text: The wrapper is a polite live region, so a label change is spoken when the person pauses. Render the meter from the first key on and keep it mounted, or some screen readers stay silent.

items.title: Label
items.text: The label replaces the default text for the level. A long text wraps under the bars, and nothing is cut.

items.title: Width
