items.text: The wrapper fills its parent and the four segments share the width equally. At 160 px the bars are about 37 px wide and the label still fits on one line.

items.title: Sample values
items.text: Use obviously made-up passwords in examples and tests, such as correct-horse. The demos run on local state and send nothing.

items.title: Dark mode
items.text: It uses theme tokens for the segments and text, so it follows the theme.

items.title: Motion
items.text: None. The segments and colour change at once when the level changes; nothing fades or slides.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: There is no motion, so reduced motion changes nothing.

minimalUsage.expected: You see an empty field. Type correct-horse and four-segment bars appear under it with three segments filled and the text Good password.

PasswordStrength.strength.description: The level to show. Required. It fills one to four segments and sets the colour. Get it from `getPasswordStrength(password)`, which returns `null` for an empty password.

PasswordStrength.label.description: The text under the bars. Defaults to the name of the level followed by `password`. Pass your own words or another language; a long text wraps.

PasswordStrength.className.description: Extra classes for the wrapper, merged after its own. Use them for a margin or a maximum width.

components.title: Backup Code
components.description: A recovery code that copies itself when clicked and is crossed out once it has been used.

parts.name: BackupCode
parts.description: A button with an 8 px radius, a 1 px border and the card fill. It is the only element: pressing it copies the code, and a used code is disabled.

parts.name: Code
parts.description: The code in 14 px medium text with tabular figures, on one line that wraps at a hyphen when the button is too narrow. A used code is struck through and tertiary.

parts.name: Copy icon
parts.description: A 14 px copy icon after the code. It is transparent until hover so it never shifts the code, and it is decorative because the code names the button.

items.text: Use Backup Code to list recovery codes after two-factor setup, in a grid with one code per button. For a single long value with a copy action, such as an invite URL, use Invite Link Row.
Mark codes that were already redeemed as used, so the list shows which ones are left. Say how many are left in text next to the grid, because the strike-through is visual only.
Confirm the copy in the copy handler, for example with a status line or a toast. It runs only after the clipboard took the code.
Offer a second way next to the list, such as Download as a text file, for the moment the clipboard is blocked.
Give each code a cell of at least 9 rem. A narrower box wraps the code at its hyphen.
Don't show your own Copied message on press. When the clipboard is blocked (an iframe, an http page, a denied permission) the copy handler does not run, and a message of your own would be wrong.
Don't rely on the copy icon to find the button. It shows on hover only, so on a touch screen the code itself is the target.
Don't use real codes in docs or tests. The demos here are made up and are not held anywhere.

useFor: Recovery codes after two-factor setup, one code per button
A short code that is copied with one press
A list that shows which codes were already used

useInstead.name: Input Group
useInstead.text: one long value, such as a link, with a visible copy button

useInstead.name: OTP Field
useInstead.text: typing a verification code instead of copying one

useInstead.name: Code Block
useInstead.text: a block of code or a command with a copy action

useInstead.name: Input
useInstead.text: a value that people edit

keyboard.intro: A code is a native button. Used codes are disabled and are skipped by the Tab key.

rows.action: Moves focus to the next or previous code that is not used.
Presses the focused code: copies it and, once the clipboard took it, calls `onCopy`.

behavior.intro: What a backup code does with state, content, the DOM and motion.

items.title: Copy
items.text: A press writes the code to the clipboard and calls the copy handler with it, but only after the write succeeded. If the page may not write, nothing happens: no callback, no message, no change.

items.title: States
items.text: A code is ready or used: hover shows the copy icon, focus draws the indigo ring, and a used code is struck through, disabled and out of the Tab order. Feedback after a copy is yours.

items.title: Long text
items.text: The button grows with its code and has no ellipsis: in a box narrower than the code the text wraps at the hyphen onto two lines. Give the code a wide enough grid cell.

items.title: Responsive
items.text: A code has no width of its own, so the grid you put it in decides. Two columns fit down to a 320 px screen; use one column for longer codes.

items.title: Names for assistive technology
items.text: The accessible name is the code, and the button has a native tooltip, Copy code. A used code is announced as unavailable but not as used, so state the count in text, for example 5 codes left.

items.title: Motion and reduced motion
items.text: The fill changes on hover and the copy icon fades in, but nothing moves. With reduced motion the colours and fade still apply, because they are not movement.

minimalUsage.expected: You should see a small bordered button with the code in it. Hover it to see a copy icon; press it to copy the code.

BackupCode.code.description: The recovery code. It is the text of the button, the accessible name and the text that is copied. Required.

BackupCode.used.description: Disables the button, strikes the code through and turns it tertiary. A used code cannot be pressed or focused.

BackupCode.onCopy.description: Called with the code after the clipboard accepted it. It is not called when the clipboard refuses, so use it for the confirmation.

BackupCode.className.description: Added to the button. Use it for the width in a grid.

components.title: Invite Row
components.description: An email field and a role picker for inviting one person, with a button to remove the row.
components.props: function InviteRow({ email, role, roles, onEmailChange, onRoleChange, onRemove, stacked, className, }: InviteRowProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: stacked
props.description: Stack email over role on small screens (Figma Type=email role stacked).

parts.name: InviteRow
parts.description: A flex container with a 12 px gap between the email and the role, with no border or fill. From the small breakpoint up they sit in one row; below that, or when stacked, one over the other.

parts.name: Email field
parts.description: An Input of type email, named Email, that takes the rest of the row. It shows the placeholder info@wunderui.com while empty.

parts.name: Role select
parts.description: A NativeSelect named Role, at least 9 rem wide, with the roles you pass. The list opens below the field.

parts.name: Remove button
parts.description: A plain icon button with a 16 px X, named Remove. It is drawn only when you pass a remove handler.

items.text: Use Invite Row for each person in a team invite list, one row per invitee. For one shareable link, use Invite Link Row.
Keep it controlled: pass the email and role with their change handlers. Without the handlers the fields don't change when someone types or picks.
Pass your own roles when the defaults (Admin, Editor, Viewer) don't match the product, and make sure the current role is one of them.
Use the stacked layout in a narrow container. The row switches layout with the screen width, not its container's, so a narrow dialog on a wide screen stays inline.
Validate in your handler and write the message under the row, like Enter a valid email address. The row has no error state, so name the address when checking several rows.
After a row is removed, move focus to the list and say which address went in a status line. Every remove button is named just Remove.
Don't pass a remove handler to a row you must keep. The remove button is drawn only when the handler exists.
Don't use real addresses in docs or tests. The addresses in the demos belong to made-up people.

useFor: A list of people to invite, one email and one role per row
A row that can be removed from the list
A role chosen from a short list

useInstead.name: Input Group
useInstead.text: one shareable link with a copy button

useInstead.name: Field
useInstead.text: a single labelled input with its own error message

useInstead.name: Select
useInstead.text: a role or option picker on its own

useInstead.name: Settings Row
useInstead.text: a setting with a title, a description and a control

keyboard.intro: A row has up to three tab stops, in this order: the email field, the role select, the remove button. The remove button exists only with a remove handler.

rows.action: Moves focus between the email field, the role select and the remove button, then on to the next row.
On the role select: opens the list.
In the open list: moves to the previous or next role.
In the open list: picks the highlighted role, closes the list and calls `onRoleChange`.
Closes the open list without a change and returns focus to the select.
On the remove button: presses it and calls `onRemove`.

behavior.intro: What an invite row does with state, content, the DOM and motion.

items.title: Controlled
items.text: The row keeps no value of its own. Typing and picking call your change handlers, and the row shows what you pass back; without a handler the field stays as it is.

items.title: Layout
items.text: From 640 px the email, role select and 36 px remove button sit in one row with a 12 px gap. Below that, or when stacked, the email is on top and the select and button under it.

items.title: States
items.text: Each control keeps the states of its own component. The row itself has no loading, error or disabled state, so write error messages yourself under the row.

items.title: Long text
items.text: A long address doesn't wrap or get cut with an ellipsis: it scrolls inside the field. Role names stay on one line in the select.

items.title: Names for assistive technology
items.text: The field is named Email, the select Role and the button Remove, the same on every row. Screen reader users can't tell rows apart by those names, so say which row changed in a status line.

items.title: Motion and reduced motion
items.text: The role list opens with a short fade and scale and leaves faster, and control colours change quickly. With reduced motion the list appears without a transition.

minimalUsage.expected: You see an email field and a role select showing Editor, side by side on a wide screen. Typing and picking change them.

InviteRow.email.description: The value of the email field. Required, and controlled: the field shows exactly this text.

InviteRow.role.description: The selected role. It should be one of `roles`. Required, and controlled.

InviteRow.roles.description: The roles in the select, as strings that are also the labels. Defaults to Admin, Editor and Viewer.

InviteRow.onEmailChange.description: Called with the new text each time the email changes. Without it the field does not change.

InviteRow.onRoleChange.description: Called with the picked role. Without it the select does not change.

InviteRow.onRemove.description: Adds the remove button and is called when it is pressed. Take the row out of your list in the handler.

InviteRow.stacked.description: Puts the email over the role and the button at every width. Without it the row stacks only below 640 px.

InviteRow.className.description: Added to the row. Use it for the width.

components.title: Settings Row
components.description: A setting's title and description with a switch, or any other control, on the right.
components.props: function SettingsRow({ title, description, control, checked, onCheckedChange, className }: SettingsRowProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: control
props.description: Trailing control: a Button, Switch, Badge … Pass `switch` props instead for the toggle variant.

parts.name: SettingsRow
parts.description: A flex row with the text on the left, the control on the right and 24 px between them, centred vertically. It has no padding, border or fill, because the list around it provides them.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The title in 14 px medium text, wrapped when long with no ellipsis. With a switch it is the name of the switch.

parts.name: Description
parts.description: The description in 12 px secondary text, 2 px under the title. Drawn only when passed.

parts.name: Control
parts.description: A switch when a checked value or change handler is set, otherwise the control you pass, such as a button, select or badge. It keeps its size and is never squeezed.

items.text: Use it for lists of preferences, one setting per row. For choices between described options use Selector Item.
Pass the checked value and a change handler for a switch. The title names the switch for assistive technology.
Pass your own control for a setting that opens something or shows a state: a Button, a Select, a Badge. Give a Switch passed this way its own aria-label, because the title cannot name it.
Pass your own Switch as the control when it must show that it is saving or disabled. The built-in switch supports neither.
Space rows with the list: a divider between rows with vertical padding on each gives one hairline between two rows, never two. Put the list in a card with a 16 px radius.
Say what changed in a status line, such as Email notifications turned off, because a switch that flips alone gives a screen reader user no other news.
Don't pass both a switch and a control. When the checked value or change handler is set, the control is ignored.
Don't put a destructive action behind a plain press. A destructive button should open a confirmation, and the result should be undoable when possible.
Don't expect the description to be announced with the switch. It is not linked to the control, so keep what matters in the title.

useFor: A list of preferences with a switch on each row
A setting that opens something: a button, a select or a badge on the right
A danger zone with a destructive button

useInstead.name: Selector Item
useInstead.text: a choice between options that each have a description

useInstead.name: Cell Switch
useInstead.text: a switch in a cell of a settings list in the mobile style

useInstead.name: Field
useInstead.text: a labelled input with a hint and an error message

useInstead.name: Switch
useInstead.text: a bare switch outside a list

keyboard.intro: The row itself is not interactive. Its control is: a switch, a button or a select, in the page's tab order.

rows.action: Moves focus to the control of the next or previous row.
On a switch: turns it on or off and calls `onCheckedChange`.
On a button in the `control`: presses it.
On a select in the `control`: opens its list. Arrow keys move, Enter picks, Esc closes.

behavior.intro: What a settings row does with state, content, the DOM and motion.

items.title: Switch or control
items.text: Setting a checked value or change handler makes the row a switch and ignores any control, otherwise it shows your control. The row keeps no value, it shows what you pass and reports what was asked.

items.title: States
items.text: The built-in switch is on or off, with the usual hover, pressed and focus states. Saving (spinner, presses ignored) and disabled (40 % dim) belong to a Switch you pass as the control.

items.title: Long text
items.text: The title and description wrap and the row grows taller, with no ellipsis. The control keeps its size and stays centred next to the text.

items.title: Responsive
items.text: The row has no breakpoints, so text and control stay side by side and the text wraps onto many lines in a very narrow row. Give a wide control its own row on a narrow screen.

items.title: Names for assistive technology
items.text: The title is the accessible name of the built-in switch, the description is not. A switch, select or button you pass as the control needs its own name.

items.title: Motion and reduced motion
items.text: The row itself has no motion. The switch handle slides with the track changing colour, and the saving spinner stops under reduced motion while the handle still moves.

minimalUsage.expected: You see the title and description on the left and a switch on the right. Pressing the switch turns it off and on.

SettingsRow.title.description: The name of the setting. It is also the accessible name of the built-in switch. Required.

SettingsRow.description.description: A line under the title that explains the setting. Optional.

SettingsRow.control.description: The control on the right when the row is not a switch: a Button, a Select, a Badge or your own Switch. Ignored when `checked` or `onCheckedChange` is set.

SettingsRow.checked.description: Turns the row into a switch and sets whether it is on. Controlled: the row does not change it.

SettingsRow.onCheckedChange.description: Turns the row into a switch and is called with the new value when it is pressed.

SettingsRow.className.description: Added to the row. Use it for the width and for the padding of a list, for example `py-3 first:pt-0 last:pb-0`.

components.title: Agenda Event
components.description: One event in an agenda list, with its start and end time, a color bar, details and guests.
components.props: function AgendaEvent({ start, end, title, meta, color, guests, onMenu, onClick, wrap, className }: AgendaEventProps): React.JSX.Element;

props.name: wrap
props.description: The title and the meta line wrap onto more lines instead of clamping (title, 2 lines) and truncating (meta). Default: false.

parts.name: AgendaEvent
parts.description: One schedule row with a line below it. With a click handler the title becomes a button stretched over the whole row, with a hover fill and a focus ring.

parts.name: Time
parts.description: The start time above an optional end time, in a fixed 64 px column, printed as written.

parts.name: Colour bar
parts.description: A 3 px bar in the event colour (one of eight, purple by default). It is always shown.

parts.name: Title
parts.description: The title, up to two lines, then an ellipsis. With a click handler it is a native button named by the title.

parts.name: Details
parts.description: A line under the title in smaller tertiary text, such as the room or call link. Cut to one line.

parts.name: Guests
parts.description: Overlapping avatars: the first three, then a +N count for the rest.

parts.name: Menu button
parts.description: A small icon button named Event menu, shown when a menu handler is set. It sits above the stretched title, so clicking it does not open the event.

parts.name: AgendaEventChip
parts.description: The compact form of an event for a day cell of a month grid: a 24 px label with a 3 px coloured bar and the truncated title. It is a button, so a Popover or Menu trigger can render it. It replaces EventChip.

items.text: Use an Agenda Event for a schedule row with guests, a menu or a detail view to open. For a plain read-only list of times and titles, use Agenda.
Pass a click handler instead of wrapping the row in a link or button. The title becomes a real button over the whole row, and the menu button stays reachable.
Keep the title short and put the place or call details on the line below it.
Give every guest a name. It becomes the avatar's hover title and the source of the initials when there is no photo.
Put rows in a bordered, rounded container with the last line removed and the outer corners rounded. Each row draws its own line below, so the last one would double the border.
Don't let the colour bar carry the meaning alone. It has no text, so name the kind of event in the title or detail line too.
Don't add overflow-hidden to the container. It clips the focus ring, which is drawn outside the row.
Don't put buttons or links inside the title or detail line. The title is already a button, and a control inside a button is invalid HTML; use the menu for extra actions.
Pass wrap where the meta line or the title runs long (phones): nothing is clamped or truncated.

useFor: A day or week schedule where an entry opens its details
Meeting lists that show who is invited
Event rows with a menu for edit, duplicate or delete

useInstead.name: Agenda
useInstead.text: a plain read-only list of times and titles

useInstead.name: Calendar
useInstead.text: a month grid, where an event shows as a small chip

useInstead.name: Timeline
useInstead.text: events that already happened, with a status and an exact date

keyboard.intro: A clickable row has one Tab stop for the title and one for the menu button; a row without a click handler has none.
keyboard.note: Arrow keys do not move focus between rows. Each button is a separate Tab stop.

rows.action: Moves focus to the next or previous button: the title of a clickable row, then its menu button.
On the title, calls `onClick` and opens the event. On the menu button, calls `onMenu` and does not open the event.

behavior.intro: What the row does with its press target, content, the DOM and motion.

items.title: One press target
items.text: With a click handler the whole row opens the event, by pointer or keyboard. Without one the row is static: no pointer cursor, no hover fill, no tab stop.

items.title: Hover and focus
items.text: A clickable row fills light grey on hover. When the title has keyboard focus, the whole row gets an indigo border and a lighter 2 px ring.

items.title: The menu does not open the event
items.text: The menu button sits above the title and stops the click, so it never opens the event. The row opens no menu itself: open yours from the menu handler and anchor it to the button.

items.title: Guests
items.text: Guests overlap with a ring in the card colour. The first three show and the rest become a +N count; a guest shows a photo if given, otherwise initials.

items.title: One line each
items.text: The title wraps to two lines, the detail line stays on one, and the time column keeps 64 px. On a narrow row the guests and menu wrap below the title.

items.title: Line below
items.text: Every row draws a line below it. Wrap rows in a bordered, rounded container, remove the last line, and don't clip the container: the focus ring would be cut off.

items.title: Colours are fixed
items.text: Eight colours: indigo, blue, purple, pink, red, orange, yellow, green. There is no custom colour, and purple is the default.

items.title: Plain markup
items.text: A row is a plain div, not a list item, so give the list a heading nearby. The bar has no text; name the event kind in the title or detail line.

items.title: Motion and reduced motion
items.text: The row adds no animation: the hover fill and the focus ring change at once. There is nothing to reduce.

minimalUsage.expected: You should see one row with the time 11:30 over 12:30, a purple bar, the title Design review and the room below it. Hover or Tab to it, then press Enter to open it.

AgendaEvent.start.description: The start time, shown in the first line of the time column. Printed as written, so format it yourself, for example `09:00`.

AgendaEvent.end.description: The end time, shown under the start time in smaller, lighter text. Leave it out for an event without a fixed end.

AgendaEvent.title.description: The name of the event, up to two lines, then an ellipsis. With `onClick` it is the label of the row's button, so write it as plain text.

AgendaEvent.meta.description: A second line under the title, in smaller tertiary text, for the room, the call link or the organiser. Truncated to one line.

AgendaEvent.color.description: The hue of the bar next to the title: `indigo`, `blue`, `purple`, `pink`, `red`, `orange`, `yellow` or `green`. Use it to tell kinds of events apart, and say the kind in the text as well.

AgendaEvent.guests.type: { name: string; initials?: string; src?: string; color?: AvatarColor }[]
AgendaEvent.guests.description: The people invited. The first three are shown as overlapping avatars, the rest as a `+N` count. `name` is the hover title, `initials` replaces the ones taken from the name, `src` shows a photo and `color` sets the avatar colour.

AgendaEvent.onClick.description: Called when the row is pressed or its title button is activated. Setting it makes the title a button over the whole row and adds the hover fill and the focus ring.

AgendaEvent.onMenu.description: Called when the `Event menu` button is pressed. Setting it shows the button at the right end of the row. It does not trigger `onClick`; open your own menu from here.

AgendaEvent.className.description: Extra classes for the row, merged after the defaults, for example to remove the line below with `border-b-0`.

AgendaEventChip.color.description: One of the eight event colours. Indigo by default.

AgendaEventChip.children.description: The title of the event, truncated to one line.

components.title: Form Actions
components.description: The row of buttons at the end of a form, aligned right, left or spread to both edges.

parts.name: FormActions
parts.description: The row. It lays its children out 8 px apart and wraps them onto a second line on a narrow screen; align sets where it sits: end (default), start or between.

parts.name: Secondary action
parts.description: The way out of the form: Cancel, Discard or Back. A plain Button that doesn't compete with the main action, and it is disabled while the main action is pending.

parts.name: Main action
parts.description: The gradient Button that submits the form, one per row. It shows pending, success or error, with a label that says what is happening.

parts.name: Destructive action
parts.description: An action that loses something, such as Delete draft. It sits at the other edge so a quick tap on the main action can't land on it; an irreversible step still needs its own confirmation.

items.text: Use Form Actions for the buttons that end a form, dialog, sheet or step. Buttons that act on the page, not the form, belong in a Toolbar.
Put the main action last, next to the way out: Cancel, then Save changes. Write both as verbs that say what happens: Create project, not OK.
Keep the DOM order equal to the screen order, so Tab follows what the eye sees. The main action comes last at the end, first when aligned to the start.
While saving, show a pending main action with its own label (Saving…) and disable the way out. Afterwards show Saved for a moment.
Put a destructive action at the opposite edge and group the other two together. Ask in an Alert Dialog before an irreversible delete.
Match the size of the fields above the row (32, 36 or 40 px) and use one size for every button in it.
Don't put two gradient buttons in a row. One main action per row; the second is a plain Button.
Don't hide the main action under a menu, and don't disable it without saying why. If there is nothing to save, say so in a status line.
Don't reorder the buttons with CSS to move the main action. Tab order stays the same and stops matching the screen.

useFor: The buttons at the end of a form: Cancel and Save
The footer of a card, a dialog or a sheet that holds a form
A bar that sticks to the bottom of a long form, or Back and Continue in a flow of steps

useInstead.name: Button Group
useInstead.text: buttons that belong to one control, such as a split or a segmented set

useInstead.name: Dialog
useInstead.text: the footer of a dialog, which lays out its own buttons with DialogFooter

useInstead.name: Toolbar
useInstead.text: commands that act on the page or a selection, not on one form

keyboard.intro: Form Actions adds no keys. Its buttons are ordinary buttons, in the order you write them.

rows.action: Moves through the buttons from left to right as they are written. A disabled button is skipped; a pending button stays in the order and is announced as busy.
Presses the focused button. A button with `type="submit"` sends the form.
In a text field of the same form, presses the first enabled submit button, so the main action does not need a click.

behavior.intro: What the row does itself, and what it leaves to the page.

items.title: A plain row
items.text: A plain flex row with an 8 px gap and centred items. It has no role and no state; the buttons carry both.

items.title: Alignment
items.text: End pushes the buttons to the end, start keeps them at the start, between splits first and last to opposite edges. With between, wrap the two end buttons in one div.

items.title: Wrapping
items.text: On a narrow screen the buttons wrap onto a second line instead of overflowing. For a deliberate column, stack them and put the main action first in the DOM.

items.title: Order
items.text: The row never reorders anything. Tab follows what you write, so write the buttons in the order they should appear.

items.title: Pending
items.text: A pending Button keeps its width and colour, shows a spinner and ignores presses, but stays focusable so the person doesn't lose their place. Disable the way out meanwhile.

items.title: Disabled
items.text: Disable Save only when there is nothing to send, and add a status line that says why. A dimmed button can't explain itself.

items.title: Sticky and footers
items.text: Make the row sticky with a border and background to keep it in view in a scrolling form, or give it a top border and subtle fill as a card footer. Round the container, not the row.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The row doesn't move. Buttons change colour quickly and the spinner turns.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: With reduced motion the spinner stops turning. The pending label still says the send is running.

minimalUsage.code:
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button"
import { FormActions } from "@/components/ui/form-actions"

export function Actions() {
  return (
    <FormActions>
      <Button type="button" variant="plain">
        Cancel
      </Button>
      <Button type="submit" variant="gradient">
        Save changes
      </Button>
    </FormActions>
  )
}
minimalUsage.expected: You see two buttons at the right end of the row, 8 px apart: a white Cancel and an indigo Save changes. Put the row at the end of a form and Save sends it.

FormActions.align.description: Where the buttons sit in the row. `end` (the default) puts them at the end, `start` at the start and `between` puts the first child at the start and the last at the end, with the space between.

FormActions.children.description: The buttons of the row, in the order they should be tabbed. With `align="between"`, give it two children and wrap several buttons of the end in one `div`.

otherExports.name: useDensity
otherExports.description: The density of the nearest `DensityProvider` and a setter for it. Outside a provider it reports the library default (`compact`) and the setter does nothing.
otherExports.summary: Reads and changes the density of the nearest DensityProvider.
otherExports.guide: Density sets the size of controls, fields and rows: `compact` (the default, controls 32–48 px) or `comfortable` (36–56 px). `useDensity` returns the density the nearest `DensityProvider` applies and a setter for it, so a settings page can offer the switch.

properties.name: density
properties.description: `"compact"` or `"comfortable"`: the density the provider applies to the document.

properties.name: setDensity
properties.description: Changes the density for the whole document. When the provider persists, the choice is written to localStorage as well. Calling it with the current value does nothing visible.

returns.description: The current density and a setter. Outside a `DensityProvider` it returns `compact` and a setter that does nothing, so a component that reads it also renders without a provider.

notes: Outside a `DensityProvider` it returns `compact` and a setter that does nothing.
The provider sets `data-density` on `<html>`, so portals such as menus and dialogs follow it. For one region only, wrap it in `<Density value>` instead.
With a `storageKey` on the provider the choice is kept in localStorage. Add `densityScript()` to the document head, so a stored `comfortable` paints before the first frame.
Switching density changes the layout without animation: the provider pauses transitions for one frame.

examples.title: A density setting
examples.description: A settings row that switches the whole document. The form below it reads the same tokens as every other control.

examples.title: Keep the choice without a flash
examples.description: The provider stores the choice. `densityScript()` applies it in the document head, before the first paint.

examples.title: Control the density yourself
examples.description: Pass `density` and `onDensityChange` to keep the value in your own state, a user profile or the URL. The hook then reports and requests changes.

useFor: A settings page or a menu that lets people choose how dense the product is.
Showing the current density somewhere, for example a checked item in a View menu.
Adapting your own layout to the density, such as the number of rows a list shows.

useInstead.name: Density
useInstead.text: one region of a page that should be denser or looser than the rest. It wraps its children and adds no box.

useInstead.name: Table
useInstead.text: row density that only one table should follow. Set it on the table card with `data-density`.

useInstead.name: DensityProvider
useInstead.text: choosing the starting density, a controlled density or the storage key. The hook only reads and sets what the provider holds.

behavior.intro: The hook reads the provider; the provider writes `data-density` on `<html>`.

items.title: State
items.text: The density lives in the nearest `DensityProvider`. `setDensity` updates it, stores it when the provider persists and calls `onDensityChange` of a controlled provider. Every component that calls `useDensity` re-renders when the density changes.

items.title: Outside a provider
items.text: Without a provider the hook returns `compact`, the library default, and a setter that does nothing. A component that only reads the density keeps working in a test or a story.

items.title: Document and portals
items.text: The provider sets `data-density` on `<html>`, so menus, dialogs and every other portal follow it. Control heights, field heights, row padding and card padding read the density tokens, so one change resizes all of them; the page grid does not change.

items.title: Storage and server rendering
items.text: With the default `storageKey` the choice is kept in localStorage under `wui-density`. Nothing touches `document` or `localStorage` while rendering, so the server and the first client render both show the default. Add `densityScript()` to the document head, so a stored `comfortable` paints before the first frame instead of jumping after hydration.

items.title: Cleanup
items.text: When the provider unmounts it removes `data-density` from `<html>` again. Mount one provider per document: two providers write the same attribute.

items.title: Motion
items.text: Switching density is a layout change, not an interaction, so it does not animate. The provider pauses all transitions for one frame, which keeps controls from sliding to their new size.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: Nothing to adapt: the switch has no motion of its own, with or without `prefers-reduced-motion`.
Offer the choice as a plain setting with two labelled options and name what changes: “Comfortable spacing”.
Do not switch the density on its own, for example by screen size. Let the person decide, and use responsive layout for the rest.
Add `densityScript()` to the head when the provider persists, so a returning visitor never sees the default first.
Do not nest a second `DensityProvider` to scope a region. Wrap the region in `Density` instead.
Read `density` for your own measurements, such as a row height of a virtual list, instead of hard-coding pixel values.
Do not store the density yourself in addition to the provider. Pass `storageKey` or control the provider.

otherExports.summary: Tells which section of a page or a scroll container is being read.
otherExports.guide: Pass the ids of the section headings. The hook returns the id of the last section whose top has passed the reading line, a quarter down the window or the container, and a setter to move the marker yourself. At the end of the scroll the last section wins, so a short closing section still becomes active.
otherExports.signature: useScrollSpy(ids: string[], root?: React.RefObject<HTMLElement | null> | undefined, enabled?: boolean): readonly [string | undefined, React.Dispatch<React.SetStateAction<string | undefined>>]

params.name: ids
params.description: The ids of the section elements, in the order they appear on the page. An id without an element in the page is ignored.

params.name: root

properties.name: current
properties.description: The current value of the ref.

params.description: A ref to the element that scrolls the sections. Leave it out when the page itself scrolls. The sections are looked up inside this element, and the reading line is a quarter of its height from its top.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Set it to `false` to stop listening, for example while the list is hidden. The marker keeps its last value.

returns.description: A tuple, like `useState`: the id being read and a setter for it.

properties.name: active
properties.description: The id of the section being read. Before the first measurement it is the first id.

properties.name: setActive
properties.description: Moves the marker yourself, usually in the click handler of a list item. The next scroll measures again and takes over.

notes: `FloatingToc` uses it when you leave out `activeId`; reach for the hook when you build your own navigation.
Pass a ref as `root` when the sections scroll inside a container instead of the window.
`enabled={false}` stops listening, for example while a drawer that holds the list is closed.
Call the setter on click so the marker moves at once, before the smooth scroll arrives.

examples.title: Inside a scroll container
examples.description: A settings panel that scrolls on its own. `root` points at the panel, so the sections are looked up inside it and the reading line is a quarter of its height.

examples.title: Track the page
examples.description: Without `root` the hook watches the window, for a long article with a table of contents beside it.

examples.title: Pause while the list is hidden
examples.description: A drawer holds the section list. While it is closed nobody sees the marker, so the hook stops listening.

useFor: Marking the current section in your own table of contents, tab list or sidebar.
A settings page whose sections scroll inside a panel, with `root` set to that panel.
Any page where the reader should always see where they are.

useInstead.name: FloatingToc
useInstead.text: a ready-made table of contents with a gliding marker. It uses this hook when you leave out `activeId`.

useInstead.name: Plain anchor links
useInstead.text: a short page where nothing needs to be marked as current.

useInstead.name: An IntersectionObserver
useInstead.text: loading or animating something once it comes into view. The hook answers which section is being read, not whether an element is visible.

behavior.intro: The hook measures on scroll and tells you one id.

items.title: State
items.text: The reading line sits a quarter down the container, or the window. The active section is the last one whose top has passed it. When the container is scrolled to its very end, the last section wins, so a short closing section can become active even though its top never reaches the line. The ids must be listed in page order.

items.title: When it measures
items.text: On every scroll event of the container (or the window) and on window resize, once at mount, and again when the list of ids, `root` or `enabled` changes. The scroll listener is passive and each measurement reads the top of each section once.

items.title: Elements and ids
items.text: Sections are found by id inside `root`, or in the document without it. A missing element is skipped, so a list that includes a section which renders later still works once it appears and the page has scrolled or resized.

items.title: Server rendering
items.text: Nothing touches `window` or `document` during render. The first value is the first id on the server and on the first client render, and the listeners start in an effect, so there is no hydration mismatch.

items.title: Cleanup
items.text: The listeners are removed when the component unmounts, when the ids or `root` change and when `enabled` becomes `false`. A disabled hook keeps the last id and does not reset it.

items.title: Motion
items.text: The hook itself does not animate. Scrolling to a section on click is yours; make it smooth normally and instant under reduced motion. Animate the marker with `transform` and `opacity` only.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: Check `prefers-reduced-motion` in the click handler and scroll with `behavior: "auto"` when it is set, as the Playground does. The hook reports the same ids either way.
List the ids in the order the sections appear on the page. The hook stops at the first section below the reading line.
Do not use it to lazy-load or to start animations. It reports the section being read, not what is visible.
Call the setter in the click handler, so the marker moves at once instead of after the smooth scroll has arrived.
Do not leave a list hidden in a closed drawer listening. Pass `enabled={open}` so nothing measures while nobody sees the result.
Mark the active item with `aria-current="location"` and give a scroll container `tabIndex={0}` and a label, so keyboard users can reach and scroll it.
Do not pass a new `root` ref on every render. Create it once with `useRef`, or the hook restarts its listeners each time.

otherExports.name: useToast
otherExports.summary: Shows, updates and closes toasts from anywhere below a Toaster.
otherExports.guide: Returns the toast manager of the nearest `Toaster`. Call `add` with a title, an optional description and a type, and the toast slides into the corner the Toaster was given. `add` returns the toast's id, which `update` and `close` take.

properties.name: toasts
properties.description: The toasts that are open right now, newest first. The component re-renders whenever the list changes.

properties.name: add
properties.description: Shows a toast and returns its id. Options: `title`, `description`, `type` (`success`, `error`, `warning`, `info`), `timeout` in ms (`0` keeps it open), `priority` (`low` or `high`), `actionProps` for an inline action such as Undo, `onClose`, `onRemove` and `id`. Adding with an id that is already open updates that toast and restarts its timer.

properties.name: close
properties.description: Closes the toast with that id. Without an id it closes every open toast.

properties.name: update
properties.type: <T extends Data = Data>(toastId: string, options: ToastManagerUpdateOptions<T> | ((prevToast: ToastObject<T>) => ToastManagerUpdateOptions<T>)) => void
properties.description: Changes an open toast in place: pass the fields to change, or a function that gets the previous toast and returns them. The toast keeps its place in the stack.

properties.name: promise
properties.type: <Value, T extends Data = Data>(promise: Promise<Value>, options: ToastManagerPromiseOptions<Value, T>) => Promise<Value>
properties.description: Shows the `loading` toast, then turns it into `success` or `error` when the promise settles. Each state is a title string or the same options as `add`; `success` and `error` can be functions of the result. Returns the promise, so you can await it.

returns.description: The toast manager of the nearest `Toaster`. The functions keep their identity between renders, so they are safe in effect dependencies; the object itself changes whenever the list of toasts does.

notes: Mount `Toaster` once, high in the tree (the root layout). Without it, `add` has nowhere to render.
`type` sets the colour of the dot: `success`, `error`, `warning` or `info` (the default).
Toasts close after 5 seconds. Pass `timeout` to keep one longer, or `0` to keep it until it is closed.
Use a toast to confirm something that already happened. A decision the user still has to make belongs in a Dialog.

examples.title: Confirm an action
examples.description: A form that saves and tells the person it worked. The toast confirms what already happened.

examples.title: Follow a request
examples.description: `promise` shows a loading toast and turns it into the result, so one call covers all three states.

examples.title: Update a toast in place
examples.description: `add` returns the id of the toast. A `timeout` of `0` keeps it open while the work runs; `update` then turns it into the result.

useFor: Confirming something that already happened: a saved profile, a copied link, a sent invitation.
Reporting the result of a request that runs in the background, with `promise`.
A short message with one optional action, such as Undo.

useInstead.name: Dialog
useInstead.text: a decision the user still has to make before anything continues.

useInstead.name: Alert
useInstead.text: a message that belongs to the page and stays until the problem is gone.

useInstead.name: Toast
useInstead.text: the toast box itself, when you render one by hand without the manager.

behavior.intro: The hook is the remote control; the toasts live in the Toaster.

items.title: State
items.text: `useToast` reads the manager of the nearest `Toaster`. Every component that calls it re-renders when the list of toasts changes, so keep the call in a small component, such as the button that triggers the toast, when the rest of the tree is heavy.

items.title: Timing
items.text: A toast closes after 5 seconds, the default of the Toaster. `timeout` on `add` changes it for one toast, `0` keeps it until it is closed. The timers pause while the pointer or the focus is inside the stack and while the browser window is in the background.

items.title: Stack and corner
items.text: Toasts stack in the corner the Toaster was given, `top-right` by default or `bottom-right`. The newest sits in front, older ones lie a little lower, smaller and fainter, and the stack opens into a list while the pointer is on it. From the fifth toast on, the older ones are hidden until a newer one closes.

items.title: Server rendering
items.text: `add`, `update`, `close` and `promise` run in the browser, in event handlers or effects. The viewport renders into a portal after mount, so a server render of the page contains no toasts and never differs from the first client render.

items.title: Cleanup
items.text: A toast belongs to the Toaster, not to the component that added it. It stays when that component unmounts, and a pending `promise` still turns its toast into the result. Close what should not outlive a screen with `close(id)` in an effect cleanup.

items.title: Announcements and keyboard
items.text: Every toast is announced to screen readers: `priority: "low"` politely (the default), `"high"` urgently, which suits errors the user must notice. Press F6 to move the focus into the stack; Tab then reaches the action and the close button of each toast, and Escape closes the toast that has the focus.

items.title: Motion
items.text: A toast slides in from the right edge and fades in over `duration-slow` with `ease-entrance`, and leaves the same way; the stack offsets and scales with the same timing when it opens. Only `transform` and `opacity` change.

items.title: Reduced motion
items.text: Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` the transform transitions are dropped, so a toast no longer slides or shifts: it fades in and out in place.
Write what happened in the title (“Changes saved”) and put the consequence or the next step in the description.
Do not put a decision in a toast. It disappears after 5 seconds, and a person who looked away cannot answer it.
Use `type: "error"` with `priority: "high"` for failures the user has to notice, and keep the message actionable: say what to try next.
Do not stack a toast per item in a loop. Add one toast that says how many items were affected.
Give a destructive action an Undo through `actionProps` and a longer `timeout`, instead of asking for confirmation first.
Do not call `add` during render. Call it in an event handler, an effect or after an awaited request.
